length set ("5m") or what is left ("04:59", five figures wide so it never moves), and a click
opens its own panel — a pane of its kind, the card a folder's grid holds at its full size, with its
countdown, its length and its name. In a grid its card is laid out for every span from one cell up (`CountdownCard`): at one
cell the tile itself starts and pauses it and the wheel sets it, a row or a column of cells has a
start button of its own, three by three its minus and plus as well, and from four by two, where a
new one starts, the whole card. In a list it is a line on the list's own edges, drawn for every
height from one row to six as every reading's line is (§9, "A line at every height"; `ListTiers`):

- **One row**: its glyph, its name, its time and its start button, a glyph alone on the trailing
  gutter. The reading wins the row — a name with no room is cut where it still reads or left out,
  its glyph saying what it is — and the button is as tall as the row leaves it under the gutter, so
  at the height a line asks for where nobody set one (`CountdownCard.LineHeight`, a little over a
  row) it has one gap on its three sides (*"on a 1-row line, the side gap matches the gap above and
  below"*). Its steppers and the button that clears it are its menu's there
  (`CountdownTile.Longer`, `Shorter`, `Stop`), and the wheel over it still sets its length.
- **The compact line**, from two rows at the list's text: the name and the time on the first row,
  and under them the steppers — or, while it runs, the button that clears it — from the text column
  and the start button with its word on the trailing gutter.
- **The whole widget**, from three: the name on its own row, the time under it at 26 DIP growing
  with the height to 36, and the buttons under that.

Which it is is what fits the height at the text size in force, not the number of rows, and a taller
line never says less than a shorter one; what is shorter than the line stands in its middle; a
glyph larger than the icon column grows into the room before the text (`ListTiers.GlyphBox`); and
the line says what it laid out, as every line does (`ILinePieces`, its main piece its time).
`CountdownFormsTests` holds every height from one row to six at 100, 150 and 200 %, every text size
and the narrowest list, and draws `list-timer.png` and `list-focus.png` beside the readings'.

**Every one is its own countdown.** *"the timer has only one store. but you should be able to add
many different timers with their own default times"*, and *"same for focus time"* (2026-09-27).

- **One countdown per widget.** What a timer or a focus session is doing is kept by its widget's
  id in the dock's `Countdowns`, in memory: any number run at once, a timer and a focus session
  side by side, and none takes over from another. A restart clears them all. The store is the
  dock's, made by it and handed to its islands, its folders and the clock's panel — never a static
  the whole process shares (a test makes its own).
- **Its own length and name.** Each widget's length — what it starts at — and an optional name
  ("Tea", "Deep work") are its settings, `CountdownOptions` in its record of `config.json`. A widget
  nobody set has no record and starts at its kind's (5 minutes, 25), so no file gains one it never
  had. The steppers and the wheel on its face set its length alone and the dock writes the config
  once the steps settle (`Countdowns.Stepped`); the Settings page sets the length in whole minutes,
  1 to 720, and the name, and shows nothing that is not a setting.
- **The name** is its label wherever its face has room for it whole — on a card or a line in its
  kind's name's place, on the panel's pane, and on the bar before the reading, where the entry is
  widened for it — and otherwise its kind's name. Once it has run out, the entry says its name in
  the figures' place where it fits there, so what rang says which one it is.
- **Carried, it keeps it all.** Moved between the taskbar, a grid and a list (`Partners`), a widget
  keeps its id, its length and its name, so a countdown that is running goes on running as what it
  became. Removed, it takes its countdown with it (`Countdowns.Keep`, on every change of the
  config).
- **The time, never cut.** The clock's panel writes the time large; at the largest text on the
  narrowest panel it was wider than the panel and ended "14:4…". The person: "shrink to fit". So
  its size steps down until it fits, chosen once for the widest the format reads (every figure an
  eight, the hour of two, both of a 12-hour clock's markers), in tabular figures, so it keeps one
  size and one place as the seconds go (`Karpo.Dock\Clock\TimeFit.cs`). A clock's line in a list
  sizes its time the same way where the line is narrow.
- **The clock's own.** The clock's panel holds the clock's own timer and focus session
  (`Countdowns.ClockKey`), apart from every widget; their lengths are the clock's options
  (`ClockOptions.TimerMinutes`, `FocusMinutes`, unwritten until set). The clock on the bar shows
  what they have left, the one running out soonest first.
- **A line each on the clock.** *"for the time widget flyout make the focus time and timer one
  liners"* (2026-10-04): as Windows 11's Focus is a line of its clock flyout, each is one line
  under the clock (`CountdownLine`, laid out by `ClockLayout`): its glyph, its name, the minus, the
  length with its unit ("25 min") or what is left ("24:13"), the plus, and the accent button that
  starts, pauses, takes up again and starts again, last. While it is set, the plus's place
  holds the button that stops it, and a thin bar along the foot of the line shows what is left —
  the accent while it counts, the quieter ink while it is paused. Both lines are laid out on one
  grid, so their buttons stand one over the other, and the time's room is the widest its lengths
  can read; nothing moves as a countdown runs. Short of room — a narrow work area, a large text
  size — the line gives way in one order (`CountdownLineTier`): the name shortens first ("Focus
  time", "Focus", "Focu…"), then goes, the glyph still saying which line it is; then the steppers
  and the stop button fold into the menu; then the glyph. The time and the start button always
  stay, and nothing runs past the line's edge. The room the two panes took and the lines do not is
  the other clocks' list's, under the most.
- **No "…" on a line.** *"for the clock flyout view, dont show the three dots, they are not
  necessary"* (2026-10-05): each line ended in a "…" that opened its menu; it is gone, and the
  start button ends the line at the gutter. The room it took is the line's, so the name shortens
  and the steppers fold later than they did. Tab stops on the line's buttons only — the minus, the
  plus (or the stop button) and the start button — and the menu is still there for whatever the
  line folded away.
- **A line's menu**: a right click anywhere on it, or the Menu key or Shift+F10 on one of its
  buttons — the keyboard's way in, on the button Tab or a click left the keyboard on
  (`ClockLineMenu`). It holds everything the line does, whether it shows it or not —
  start or pause, stop, a minute longer and a minute shorter, each enabled where it would do
  something now — and, on the focus session's, "Turn on do not disturb", ticked while the clock's
  `ClockOptions.FocusDoNotDisturb` is on and written at once when it is switched. The dock shows it
  as it shows every menu of Karpo's, and the clock stays open behind it; a press that closes the
  menu outside the clock closes the clock too.
- **A focus session turns on do not disturb** while it runs, as Windows 11's Focus does
  (`FocusQuiet`, through the one service the bell shares, §18): on when it starts, off when it runs
  out or is stopped, and a pause keeps it. Where it was on before the session, or the person
  switched it during it — off, or to alarms only, anywhere — it is theirs and the end leaves it as
  it is; several sessions hold it together until the last one ends, and the dock going ends them
  all. Windows is asked nothing until a session starts, and where it has not said yet what do not
  disturb is, the session waits for the answer rather than guess what it was before. It is each
  focus-time widget's "Turn on do not disturb" (`CountdownOptions.DoNotDisturb`), and the clock's
  for its own focus session (`ClockOptions.FocusDoNotDisturb`): on unless somebody turned it off,
  so only an off is written. `FocusQuietTests` holds all of it on the service's made-up source.
- **Running out.** Each rings once, with Windows' notification sound, and several in one second ring
  once between them; its face says it is over, in the accent, and by its name. Nothing opens for
  it. In a folder that is shut — where nothing opens a popup (§15) — the folder's button wears an
  accent dot on its corner until it is opened (`FolderIsland.Due`).
- **A menu** — a folder's right-click on a card too small for its buttons — works it through
  `CountdownTile.Act` and `CountdownTile.Stop`: its start button and the button that clears it,
  the same rules its buttons press, on its own countdown; and, as "A minute longer" and "A minute
  shorter", through `CountdownTile.Longer` and `Shorter`, its plus and its minus, which do nothing
  while it runs (`CountdownTile.Steps` says when either would change its length, and the rows are
  enabled by it).

### The pieces

- **Face.** A folder's button is drawn by a widget of the user's choosing. The
  face is a widget **instance**, not a kind: a clock face has its own time zone
  and format, so the folder's config carries an island for it beside its cells,
  and the folder measures the face rather than its square where one is set. The
  2×2 preview stays the default where no face is chosen.

  **The cell is fixed at 36 DIP** (`FolderOptions.CellPx`), a cell of the
  taskbar's own grid: the person tried the sizes that were offered and asked for
  one number instead, so the setting and its stepper are gone and an older file's
  size is read, ignored and dropped. It halved every cell, which the chrome drawn
  inside one had to follow: the "+" in a free place already scaled with the cell,
  and the resize grip did not — measured from the panel's text it covered 52% of a
  one-cell card and took 81% of it as its target, so it is measured from the card
  now (at most 42% of its shorter side for the mark, 55% for the target) and a
  card spanning more cells still gets the comfortable grip.

  **Built.** `FolderOptions.Face` is an `Island?`, absent until somebody chooses
  one, so a file written before faces existed says "no face" by leaving the key
  out and no migration is needed. What was learnt building it:

  - **"Anything that opens a panel of its own" could not be the rule.** The clock
    opens a calendar today, and the clock is the example this whole section was
    written for. The face never receives the click, so what it would open is
    never opened, and the rule that survives is the cells' own: a face is
    anything the taskbar can draw that is not a container
    (`Sections.CanFace` = `OnBar && !IsFolder`). When no widget owns a flyout any
    more the two readings agree and nothing changes.
  - **The face is measured, not guessed.** `WidgetShapes.Folder` returns the
    face's own shape, so a date face makes the folder exactly as wide as a date.
    The painting asks the same question through the same function
    (`FolderIsland.FaceDrawn`), because a button measured as a face and drawn as
    a glyph is the bug that sharing the numbers exists to prevent.
  - **One cell.** A folder's button is a button, so a face whose shape wants more
    than one cell (the media widget with its transport buttons) falls back to the
    square, as does a face of a kind nobody has given a shape — that one would
    have to be measured from a live island, and the button is measured from the
    config alone. Both fall back to the glyph and the 2×2 preview, which is what a
    folder without a face looks like: the button is never blank, and never the
    wrong width.
  - **The name is not drawn beside a face.** A name beside a clock face reads as
    that clock's label, and it doubles the button's width for a word the open
    folder's own footer already says. `ShowName` is kept, so taking the face off
    brings the name back.
  - **The face's own settings are inlined.** They stand on the folder's page under
    a heading that names the face ("Date", "Clock"), and they are the very cards
    that widget has on its own page, shown for a second options object pointed at
    the face. A link to a page of its own was the first attempt and the user threw
    it back: setting a date's format should not mean leaving the folder. The face
    is still found at "<folder id>/face", which is what the second options object
    edits and what a deep link would reach.
  - **One width.** The folder's is the only one: its block on the bar is the
    folder's and the face is drawn inside it, so a face carries no width at all —
    not one from a file, and not the kind's default that the repair hands to a
    widget with none (`CarryOverWidth` is deliberately not called for a face).
    There is no second row to hide or disable, and nothing keeps a value with no
    effect. The folder's width row says where the face stands in relation to it.
  - **It ticks on the bar.** The widgets in a folder tick only while it is open;
    the face is what the folder looks like while it is **shut**, so it ticks
    there, and the folder redraws when the face says something changed. A folder
    without a face still has an interval of 0, exactly as before.
- **Faces are draw-only.** A folder's button opens the folder, so the face never
  receives the click — a Wi-Fi switch as a face would not toggle. The folder's
  settings say so where the face is chosen, rather than leaving it to be found.
- **The same widget twice is two instances.** A folder whose face is a clock and
  which also contains a clock has two clock islands. An island carries per-instance
  state (its options, its tick); one object drawn twice would share it.
- **Leaves.** The collapsed views and the panel contents are ordinary widgets.
  Nothing about a graph, an app list or a day switcher is special.
- **Presets.** A catalogue entry can create a folder, its face and its contents in
  one act, so someone who adds "Clock" gets the finished thing rather than a kit.
  The recipe is **data on the descriptor**, not code in the settings app, because
  the bar's "+" and the settings catalogue must produce the identical thing.

  **Built** (`Karpo.Core\Presets.cs`). A preset is its own descriptor beside the
  kinds — `WidgetPreset`, in `Presets.All` — rather than a field on `WidgetKind`,
  because "Clock" the composition and "Clock" the kind are two catalogue rows on
  two pages and one descriptor cannot be both. The recipe stays pure data; the one
  act that turns it into an island, `Presets.Expand`, is in **Karpo.Core**, which
  is the honest reading of "not code in the settings app": neither app decides
  what a preset holds, and the identity the section asks for is structural rather
  than agreed. When this was written the bar's "+" launched the settings catalogue,
  so there was only one path; the dock has its own add list now (§7b). What was learnt building it:

  - **No config shape changes, so there is nothing to migrate.** A preset is never
    stored — only what it expands to is, and that is an ordinary folder island with
    ordinary widgets in its cells. A file written before presets existed and one
    written after are the same file, and the guard is a test that expands each
    preset, saves it, reads it back through `Config.Repair` and finds every widget
    still in the place the recipe gave it.
  - **The arrangement is part of the recipe.** Each cell names its column, row and
    span, rather than being handed to `Folders.Add` in order: a preset is an
    arrangement somebody chose, and one that falls out of a list's order is one
    nobody chose. The clock's three-by-three is filled exactly, nine cells for
    nine, which a test holds.
  - **A bad recipe throws rather than dropping half of itself.** A face that may
    not be one, a container in a cell, a folder kind that is not a folder: inside
    the boundary every value came from this build's own data, so each is a mistake
    in the list and not an old file (§5). A preset that quietly lost three of its
    five widgets would be found by the person, once, with no way to say why.
  - **A preset cannot be added to a folder, and is refused with a reason** rather
    than flattened into its parts (`Presets.NotInAFolder`, shown on the greyed row
    as every other refusal is). Adding the contents flat was the alternative and it
    is worse in three ways: it delivers something other than what the row promised,
    it can overflow the target grid so you get *some* of them, and the person
    cannot tell which. The pieces are one page away on Components.
  - **Two, not twenty.** *Clock* — a grid folder behind a clock face holding the
    clock, the date, a calendar, a timer and focus time, which is exactly what
    clicking the clock gives you today. *Quick settings* — a row folder behind the
    battery holding Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, the volume button, airplane mode and power;
    part of that is drawn on the bar and nowhere else, so no grid and no list could
    hold the set, which makes it a composition nobody could have assembled another
    way. A third is a record in `Presets.All`.
  - **A second face is not a second preset.** "Calendar" as the same five widgets
    behind a date face was the tempting third, and it is a *setting* of the folder
    somebody placed, not another row in the catalogue. That is the line that keeps
    two presets from becoming twenty.
- **Two pages, in the user's words.** *Widgets* are what a person places — the
  precomposed compositions and the simple kinds where placing one is already the
  finished thing. *Components* are the pieces a composition is made of. A kind
  says which it is offered as (`Offer`: Widget, Component, or Both — a clock face
  is a component and also a perfectly good thing to have bare on a bar). This is a
  different axis from `Surfaces`, which keeps meaning only *where a kind can be
  drawn*; a component that cannot be drawn where you are adding is already greyed
  with its reason, so the catalogue needs no second mechanism to keep people out
  of trouble.

  **Built** (`WidgetKind.Offer`, and the pages in `Karpo.Core\Catalogue.cs`). It is
  a flags enum whose values *are* the pages, so "which page is this row on" is one
  `HasFlag` rather than a mapping between two enums that can drift, and it is
  **null** for the legacy kinds — offered on neither page — for the reason
  `Preview` is null for them, with `Widgets.OfferOf` throwing rather than guessing.
  What was learnt:

  - **A shadowed kind must stay reachable, and that has to be checkable.** "Clock"
    on the Widgets page is now the composition, so the bare clock is offered as a
    `Component` and nowhere else — one page away, never two rows of the same name
    in one list. The preset says which kind it stands in for (`Replaces`), and a
    test holds the two answers together, so a kind cannot drift back onto the
    Widgets page and a new preset fails until its shadowed kind is updated.
  - **The face is not the same question.** The quick-settings folder wears a
    battery, and a battery bare on a bar is still a finished thing, so `Replaces`
    is null there and Battery stays on both pages. Deriving the shadowing from the
    face would have been the tempting shortcut and it is wrong.
  - **The two pages are not far apart, and that is honest.** Most kinds are `Both`:
    a kind is `Widget` only where nothing composes with it (the bar's own
    furniture, and the folders themselves, which cannot be pieces because folders
    do not nest), and `Component` only where placing one bare is not a finished
    thing (a kind no bar can draw, or one a preset replaced). Whether the
    Components page should be leaner than that is a judgement about somebody
    else's taskbar, and it is one field per kind when it is made.
  - **Search is per page, and says what the other page holds.** Two pages means a
    search on one of them can leave somebody sure a kind has gone, so a page says
    "“clock” also matches 1 component." and clicking that line goes there keeping
    the words (`CatalogueSearch.AlsoOn`). Within a page there is nothing to tell
    apart — the composition and the bare kind are never in one list — and a
    composition wears a small folder at its row's trailing edge, because one click
    on it makes five widgets and the page you are on is a weak way to learn that.

### What this is not

**A destination, not an invariant.** Twenty-one placeable kinds own a flyout
today, and each one stops owning it at its own conversion — not before. A test
that asserts "no kind opens a flyout" would fail on twenty of them.

And the conversions are **large and unequal**: screen time is 1,424 lines,
notifications 998, the calendar 849, the weather 623. Converting the calendar is
a redesign of the calendar, not a re-housing of its code. "Screen time first, and
then the others" should not be read as one job repeated.

### Order

**Stage 1 and 2 are built (screen time).** What they taught, for the conversions that follow:

- **A component out of a panel declares at least two rows.** Below about 55 DIP a card is drawn
  the way the bar draws it (`TilePaint.CardFits`), and a component lifted out of a panel has no
  bar drawing at all — one row of a 36 DIP cell shows its kind's glyph and nothing else.
- **A grid's rows reach twelve, its columns still six** (`FolderOptions.MostRows`). A grid holds
  about a panel: that is the constant's meaning, and it is what stayed the same when the cell
  became 36 DIP. Twelve rows with their gaps and the grid's pad is 544 DIP, which is what the
  screen-time panel stands at. A folder taller than the display still scrolls, as every folder
  already did, because the panel is never more than 70% of the work area.
- **The conversion re-houses a panel, it does not redraw it.** The four seams:

  1. **Split the panel's painters along the regions** you want as components, and leave the
     whole-panel painter calling them, so the old panel goes on working while you convert.
  2. **Give the panel's plan the surroundings it lays itself out against**, so a component can
     build the same plan for its card. A width was enough for screen time, whose height is a sum
     of its parts; it was not enough for notifications, whose height is a **rule** (as tall as its
     cards, up to 70% of the work area) — a card has no work area, and passing the card's height
     as the work height would have given the card seven tenths of itself and left the rest blank,
     so that panel's plan takes a cap as well. The general form: **a plan that computes its own
     size from its surroundings needs those surroundings passed in, not inferred**, or the
     component lays out against itself.
  3. **One `CellIsland` per panel**, with a part enum and a `RegionOf(plan, part)`. Ask first
     **what space this panel's pieces are laid out in**: screen time's rows are in *panel*
     coordinates, so its tile shifts everything by the region's top; notification rows are in
     *list* coordinates, so its tile places rows at their own boxes and uses the region only for
     the clip and the empty state. Neither is wrong, and the answer decides the tile's whole shape.
  4. **A `WidgetSource` and a registry entry per component**, with `Surfaces.Grid`,
     `Offer = Component`, `MinGrid` of at least two rows, `Options = None`, `Click = Nothing` and
     `Tooltip = false` — plus the three test lists that hold new kinds to account.
- **The migration is the flip.** A preset says what the folder holds and how it is arranged
  (`Presets`, `Replaces` moves the bare kind to Components), and a gated migration replaces the
  placed widget with that folder, **keeping the widget as the face** — its id, its place, its
  options and its width. Nothing is deleted, and the dock needs no change at all: the island on
  the bar is a folder, so a click opens a folder.

**Notifications, converted on those seams.** All four fitted, and what they did not cover is
worth as much as what they did:

- **How many components is the panel's question, not the template's — and the test is whether
  each can stand alone.** This went three (header, list, footer link), then two (the list and a
  "Clear all" beside it), then **one**, on the person's own words: "dont show a clear button of
  the notifications widget by itself". "Clear all" is a control **of** the list — it is where the
  panel has it, on the band above the cards — and a piece that cannot stand alone was never a
  piece. The title is not one either (the folder's footer says what the folder is, the argument
  that keeps a name from being drawn beside a face) and "Notification settings" is a way out to
  Windows. Screen time's three were three *subjects*; a panel's chrome is not a subject, and
  splitting along the bands rather than along the subjects is how you get one component too many.
- **A panel that bounds itself by the work area needs one more parameter than a width.** The
  notifications panel is as tall as its cards up to 70% of the work area; a card has no work area to
  take a share of, so the plan takes `Capped` beside `WidthDip` and a card hands its own height
  in as the viewport. Seam 2 as written ("let the plan take a width") is not quite enough for a
  panel whose height is a rule rather than a sum.
- **The height is two questions, and the list folder is what keeps them apart.** Converting into
  a *grid* would have cost the one thing this panel was built for: the panel is as tall as its
  contents, a grid is as tall as its cells, so a quiet day would have given the same panel as a
  busy one. A **list folder** is the mechanism rather than an exception — its height follows what
  is in it, live. The other question is the line's own room, and its answer is the opposite: a
  line is as tall as its widget declared, so the card does not grow because notifications
  arrived, and what does not fit is summarised in the line's last row ("Filling the room"). Both
  are §9's, and they are about different things — how many lines there are, and how tall a line is.
- **The seams say nothing about the pointer, and a re-housed panel is full of it.** Hover is
  per-component state — two cards must not agree about which row is hot — so the shared-state
  seam is the wrong shape for it, and `FolderFlyout.HoverOver` tells a widget where the pointer
  is and then draws nothing. A component asks for its own redraw with `CellIsland.Wake`, which
  is the path a widget's news already takes out of a folder. The cheaper answer is for the
  flyout to redraw the card it just told; that is one line in somebody else's file.
- **A list folder did not offer a widget the pointer at all**, and that was found by converting
  into one. `Activate`, `TakePointer`, `WheelOver`, `HoverOver` and `FocusedWidget` each returned
  early on `FolderView.List`, because a list's line used to be the folder's own drawing.
  `ListRowsOf` made that false: a line taller than one row draws the **widget's** card, and the
  same condition had to reach the pointer or the card was a picture. Every action a converted
  panel has — dismissing one notification, clicking through to its app — was behind it.
- **Having more than fits was the one thing the seams did not cover, and the shared answer took
  it.** A list of notifications has more than fits by nature, so this is the component that needed
  `WidgetFill` most; it hands over the row heights, the summary row's height and the room, and
  draws what comes back. **The order is all it contributes**: the notifications are newest first,
  so the summary stands for the *oldest*. Screen time's "other apps" summarises the smallest
  shares and this summarises the oldest arrivals — the same rule ("summarise the tail as
  ordered"), reached for different reasons. A mechanism that summarised by some idea of importance
  instead would have to be told what importance means per kind.
- **A summary row is a statement, not a control.** Nothing leads anywhere from it, because the
  folder is already showing everything it has to say. That is also why the kind's `Interaction`
  went back to `Click`: a component that does not scroll has no claim on the wheel, and leaving
  it claimed would have stopped the panel under it scrolling for nothing.
- **A component may not draw the folder's own vocabulary, and the split is what enforces that.**
  Merging "Clear all" into the list did not stop it reading as a second widget, because the
  component went on drawing the panel's header hairline — edge to edge, in the divider colour,
  which is exactly how a list folder says *"these are two stacked widgets"*. The same ink in the
  same place meant two different things, and the person reported it twice before anyone looked at
  the drawing rather than at the config.

  The rule that prevents it is structural rather than a discipline, and seam 1 already contains
  it when the split is made in the right place: **a converted panel's painters divide into region
  painters and a whole-panel painter, and a component may only call the region ones.** The
  panel's own chrome — its band dividers, its title, its footer — lives in the whole-panel
  painter, so no component can inherit it. Screen time was clean from the start for exactly this
  reason; notifications was not, because "Clear all" was moved into a region painter along with
  the line above it. *If a component has to call something that draws the panel's chrome, the
  split is in the wrong place.*

  Two things that make an audit harder than it looks. The divider colour is not itself the
  vocabulary: screen time's donut draws its unfilled track in `theme.Divider`, and a ring is not
  a line — grepping for the colour finds it and it is fine. And what is checkable is the other
  half of the question: a one-line list folder draws no lines at all, so any full-bleed line
  inside it is the component's.
- **A picture tells you where to measure, and never what the number is.** The offscreen sheets
  earned their keep on this conversion by catching things nothing asserted — and nearly paid for
  it three times over by producing wrong fixes. Two people, a day apart, read the same thumbnail
  and were certain the notification summary row's foot was being clipped; a measurement and then
  a pixel scan both said it clears by a gap, and the light theme's near-invisible `CardStroke`
  against the footer's shade was the whole of the illusion. The test written to settle it
  (`TheSummaryRowIsDrawnWhole`) is worth more than the fix it prevented, because the defect it
  guards — placing a summary where the next row would have started and counting the gap once
  instead of twice — is real and invisible without a picture.
- **A sheet that draws live data is not a guard.** The notifications sheet showed three cards on
  one machine and the empty state on the next, because it read the real store. A component takes
  its data from one place, so that is where a fixture goes in: `NotificationPartTile.Shown`
  beside the weather's `Source`, and `Clock.Now()` — the dock's own seam, which screen time's
  cards already read — pinned alongside it, so the times read "Now / 7m / 28m / 1h" rather than
  eight identical dates. Deterministic and representative are two requirements, and a fixture in
  the past satisfies only the first.
- **A per-group cap on the catalogue cannot survive the conversions.** Every panel converted puts
  its pieces on the Components page, and that page's length is decided by how many regions the
  panels have. The cap now holds against the **Widgets** page only; the Components page is
  checked for empty groups instead, since an empty heading was the real defect.

**Sound, the fourth, found that the seams assume a kind of panel.** Ask **which kind of panel this
is** before reaching for seams 1 to 3, because there are two kinds and only one of them is what
those seams were written from.

- Screen time, notifications and the weather are **painter panels**: a `Plan` of rectangles and a
  set of `Paint*` methods over it. Seam 1 splits the painters, seam 2 hands the plan its
  surroundings, seam 3 asks which space the plan's rectangles are in.
- The sound panel is a **retained-control page** (`SoundPage : QuickPage`). `Build(PageLayout)`
  places toolkit controls — `Label`, `Button`, `Slider`, `ListRow`, `Backdrop`, `Keyed<T>` — and
  each control paints itself through `Paint(dc, QuickContext)`. There is no plan and no painter.
  Every quick-settings page is this kind; the Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, battery, media and power panels
  are all still to come.

For a page of that kind the first three seams read differently, and pretending otherwise costs
hours:

1. **There are no painters to split.** What splits is the *placement* code, and what a component
   inherits is the controls, not a drawing. The rule behind the seam survives — re-house, do not
   redraw — but it is kept by hosting the same controls in the card, not by calling the same
   painter.
2. **The plan does not take a width; it derives one.** `PageLayout` fixes `Width` at
   `Flyout.PanelWidthDip` (360) and takes `maxHeight` and `scrolled` instead. Its body height is a
   sum, but the cap that makes it a rule is applied *outside* the page, in `QuickPanel.Set`. So
   the parameter a component needs is not the one seam 2 names, and the thing to pass in is the
   card's own box.
3. **There is not one coordinate space but four** — header, body content, footer, and an `Over`
   layer in panel pixels. A card has the first three in some form and **cannot have the fourth**:
   `Over` exists to draw on top of a panel, and a card has no panel to draw on top of.
4. **Seam 4 fits unchanged.** A `WidgetSource` and a registry entry per component, `Surfaces.List`,
   `Offer = Component`, `Options = None`, `Click = Nothing`, `Tooltip = false`, a `MinGrid` of at
   least two rows with `MinGrid.Columns = 1`, and the test lists that hold a new kind to account.

Two consequences worth having in advance:

- **Anything drawn in the `Over` layer cannot come across.** The sound panel's device pickers are
  inline dropdowns drawn there precisely so the panel does not resize, and a card may not grow
  either (see "Filling the room"). The answer is not to port the dropdown but to delete it: the
  **list becomes the component** — the devices as rows, the one in use marked, pick to switch,
  filling and summarising like any other. That deletes a state (`outputOpen`) rather than moving
  it, and it is the notifications lesson again, where the list was the component all along.
- **A component may already exist.** The sound panel's master volume is `BarKind.Volume`, a widget
  that has been on the bar and in folders all along, with the drag and the wheel already declared
  and `CardPress`/`CardDrag`/`CardRelease` already written. Minting a component for it would have
  been a second drawing of one subject, which is §7a's whole complaint. "A piece that cannot stand
  alone was never a piece" reads forwards as well as backwards: before splitting a region out, ask
  whether a widget for it is already shipping.

Screen time first and alone: the flyout becomes a folder invisibly, then its
panel becomes three components, then the face, then folder-owned selection, then
overflow. Nothing else converts until that one is running. Each conversion brings
a gated, idempotent migration that moves an existing widget into the new shape and
**never deletes anything** — a widget someone placed survives as a widget
somewhere. The default arrangement of a converted panel is proposed with a picture
before its migration is written, because it is cheap to choose now and permanent
afterwards.

### Channels (shared state)

A month calendar and an agenda in one folder agree on "Thursday" without knowing about each other:
the **folder** holds the day and the widgets publish and follow it through the container. It is
**transient** — it resets when the folder closes. A month that wrote the config on every click
would be a disk-churn bug diagnosed from a report three weeks later.

**Built as channels** (2026-10-09; `Karpo.Core\Channels.cs`, `Karpo.Dock\Islands\WidgetContainer.cs`).
The person: "the widgets now need a way to synchronize, e.g. if you select a date on the calendar it
should show the correct events for that day … as generic as possible so that other combinations are
possible as well." A **channel** is a named, typed value (`Channel<T>`) in one registry
(`Channels.All`); the first is **Day** (`Channel<DateOnly>`, unset = today). Which widget publishes
and which follows is its list record's answer (`ListWidget.Publishes`, `ListWidget.Follows`): the
month publishes and follows the day, the calendar's agenda follows it, and screen time's total
publishes and follows it and its apps follow it (§69). A new pairing is a channel in
the registry and two words in two records; nothing names both widgets.

**App and App hover** (2026-10-10; `Channel<AppId>`, unset = no app). The person, of screen time:
"when you click on an application it should not open it but select it ... this does not get shared
with other widgets yet but it should. both states, hover and selected." **App** is the app picked in
the folder; **App hover** the app the pointer is on, in whichever widget, while it is there. An
`AppId` is the app's key (an executable's path, or `aumid:` and the AppUserModelID — screen time's
`ScreenTimeApps.KeyOf`), one app whatever the case of its path; any widget that shows apps can follow
either. Screen time's total and apps publish and follow both (§69). A value can be **taken back**
(`ChannelValues.Unset`, `IWidgetContainer.Withdraw`, `CellIsland.Withdraw`): the pointer leaving an
app, a pick let go. For a channel whose unset means something (no app) a widget reads the folder's
value only where it follows it (`CellIsland.Following`), else its own. **Escape** takes back the
channels marked `Channel.Escapes` — the app picked — before it closes the folder: the first Escape
lets the pick go, the second closes (`FolderIsland.Escape`, asked by `FolderFlyout.Message` ahead of
the host's own Escape); the day is where the folder is, not something picked, and stays. Both reset
when the folder closes, as the day does. Their switches: "Follow the folder's app" and "Light the
app pointed at", on.

Rules:

- **A widget never needs a container.** `Container` is null everywhere but a folder; `Followed`
  answers null (the channel's default: today) and `Publish` does nothing. A month on its own picks
  today; an agenda on its own lists today and what is coming.
- **The channel carries the type**, and a value that is not what the channel says reads as unset
  rather than throwing — a disagreement degrades to no value, never to a wrong one.
- **A follower may opt out.** Each channel a widget's kind follows is a switch on its Settings page
  ("Follow the folder's day", on), stored as the ids switched off (`WidgetItem.Unfollowed`, absent
  while it follows everything). A widget that does not follow reads the default; a month that does
  not follow keeps a day of its own and still publishes.
- **The container redraws what the container changed.** `Publish` raises the folder's own change,
  which the open panel already draws from; publishing what is there already draws nothing.

  A card with **pointer feedback of its own** — a month lighting the day under the pointer —
  changes nothing shared and must still be drawn again; that redraw belongs to the folder at the
  moment it tells the card where the pointer is: `HoverOver` draws the card it has just told.
- **State that is already global does not belong in a channel.** What the notifications agree about
  is the notification store, which is wider than any folder. A channel is for what a folder's widgets
  agree about *because they are in that folder*.

Tests: `ChannelsTests` (the registry, values per channel and type, publishing the same value, clearing,
which records publish and follow, the opt-out and its round trip), `FlyoutLinesTests` (a click on a day
publishes it and the agenda shows that day's events; the folder closing forgets it; an agenda switched
off keeps to today; a second channel of another type through the same folder; two months agree; the
keys and the wheel).

### The pointer in a folder

A folder **routes the pointer to the widget under it**. A card is not a picture with a click on
it: the volume slider is dragged in a folder, the media buttons are pressed, the day switcher's
arrows step, a notification is dismissed by its own ×. Without this a converted panel draws
correctly and does nothing, which is how it was found.

Two halves, and they are deliberately different kinds of thing:

- **The widget declares what it may take where it stands** (`Interaction`, on its `BarEntry`,
  `GridWidget` or `ListWidget`, which the island its factory makes carries as
  `CellIsland.Interaction`): `Click`, `Drag` — a press inside it may be its own rather than the
  start of a move — and `Wheel` — a turn over it is its own, and the surface under it does not
  scroll. The bar reads its entry's and a folder its card's or line's, one declaration each, so
  there is one answer to who takes a gesture where. `is ISliderIsland` was that answer once, and an answer given by omission is how
  a kind inherits behaviour it never asked for.
- **The widget says where** (`CellIsland.CardTarget`, `CardPress`, `CardDrag`, `CardRelease`,
  `CardWheel`, `CardHover`, `CardKey`), and the folder asks through one way in per gesture
  (`TargetOn`, `PressOn`, `DragOn`, `ReleaseOn`, `WheelOn`, `HoverOn`, `KeyOn`). The bar's branch
  is not virtual, so no kind can answer for a row.
- **On the bar, a widget without a slider may still take the wheel and the middle click**
  (`IWheelIsland`, `IMiddleClickIsland`): the sound icon steps the volume two a notch under the
  wheel and mutes on a middle click, as Windows 11's does. **The volume's tick waits for the wheel
  to rest**: a run of notches — on the sound icon, a flyout's volume slider, the volume card or its
  list line, or arrow keys on a slider — plays one tick `Feedback.QuietMs` (300 ms) after its last
  notch (`Feedback.Notch`), as Windows does, not one a notch; a drag let go ticks at once. **The
  tick is played at the level just set** (2026-10-08: it *"always has the same volume"*): every
  caller sets the level first and hands `Feedback` the level the output now has, and Karpo plays
  the Default Beep itself (`PlaySound`, `SND_SYSTEM`, the system sounds' session on the default
  output, which the master level scales) rather than through `MessageBeep`. Its entry says `Wheel`, so the bar asks
  it; Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, drawn by the same class, say only `Click` and are never asked. A middle
  click a widget does not take is the click it always was. Their right click has Windows' own rows
  over the common ones (`ActsFor(BarKind)`, Dock.WidgetMenus.cs): the sound icon's "Open volume
  mixer", "Sound settings" and "Troubleshoot sound problems", the network icon's "Diagnose network
  problems" and "Network and Internet settings", the battery's "Power & battery settings".

Three rules hold it together:

- **Painting and hit-testing ask the same question.** `CardDrawn` decides which drawing is on the
  screen, and the press, the drag, the wheel, the hover and the keys all read it. Two code paths
  each correct about its own half is the §2 defect, and it bit here exactly: a row folder drew the
  bar's cells and hit-tested them with the card's geometry, so a click near a track's title could
  pause the music.
- **A list is not an exception.** `FolderFlyout.DrawsOwnCard` answers "does the widget draw this
  line" for the click, the hover, the pointer a widget takes and the keyboard's widget — the same
  question the drawing asks (`Sections.CardInList`). Four places used to return early on a list
  because a list's line was once always the folder's own drawing, and a converted panel then drew
  correctly and responded to nothing.
- **Pointer feedback is the folder's redraw, not the widget's.** A card lighting the row under the
  pointer changes nothing shared and cannot reach the surface it is drawn into, so `HoverOver`
  draws the card it has just told. See "Shared state" above for why that is not the container's job.
- **A line lights as a list's row does.** Under the pointer a grid's card is its card's fill
  lightened; a list's line wears no card, so it lights with the subtle fill alone, as the rows of
  Windows' lists and of Karpo's menus do (`FolderFlyout.FillOf`, `InkOf`). It used to light with
  the card's hover, the subtle fill blended into a card of seven tenths white, which on the light
  theme's panel came out within five levels of the panel: a pin's line in a list seemed not to
  light at all (backlog 21). `ListLineLookTests` holds a line's hover at least as far from the
  panel as a menu row's, in both themes. A heading never lights: it is not a thing to press.
  That was half of it. A line at rest wore no brush at all, and the compositor does not draw again
  a sprite shape with neither fill nor stroke that is given a fill later: the line was hot and the
  screen never showed it. A line at rest wears a clear brush instead, and `ListLineHoverShots`
  captures the real folder on a hidden desktop and holds each pin's line lit on the screen.
- **A widget made of rows lights a row, never itself** (2026-10-04: "the folder contents widget
  when hovered over shows the whole widget in the hover state, this should not be, just the
  folders should have the hover over state"). A widget whose rows light under the pointer
  themselves says so (`CellIsland.LightsItsRows`), and the folder then leaves its card or its line
  as it is at rest, under the pointer and pressed (`FillOf`'s `still`): a lit line with a lit row
  on it read as two things to press. A pin showing its folder's contents (its items; it was the
  folder widget, §32), the removable devices (a
  device and its eject button), the notification list (a notification, its close button, "Clear
  all") and the sound lines (a device, the controls) say it; a click beside their rows does what it
  did. A widget that is one thing to press — a pin, a switch, the drive, whose whole card is
  its one target — still lights whole. While the folder is arranged a card lights whole whatever
  it is, as a press there picks the whole widget up. On the bar the same pin is a row of buttons,
  each lit as an app button is (§32; `FolderWidgetHoverTests`).
- **Only what acts lights** (2026-10-11: "the widgets in the list view should not have a hover over
  animation, but all the logic subitems that have an logic/ action behind them"). A line lights
  as a whole only where the whole of it is the one thing a press does (`FolderFlyout.LightsWhole`):
  its click acts (`CellAct.Action`) and it is not made of rows that light themselves, or it is not
  set up and the whole of it is its "Set up in Settings". So the pin (just itself), the switches,
  the five graphs and their details (Task Manager), Security, a drive (just itself) and the
  network drive, the weather's three lines (a search for the weather; the conditions' refresh
  button lights on its own as well), Task view, the Snipping Tool, Settings and the power buttons
  light whole. Every other line keeps still — what's playing, the brightness and the sound lines,
  the timer, focus, stopwatch and alarm, the clock, the calendar's lines, a stock, the battery,
  the notes and the to-do list, the quick-settings pages, the toggles and the actions, the
  desktops, the clipboard, mail, the feeds, contacts, the notifications, screen time — and only its
  own buttons, rows, chips and thumbs light, each on its own and pressed while held: the media
  line's transport, shuffle, repeat and picker wear the subtle button's plate; the brightness
  thumb's core grows and shrinks as the panel's slider's does. Arranging is apart: there every
  line lights whole (`LineHoverRuleTests`, which holds every kind and the real folder on a hidden
  desktop).

**The countdown took it up.** The timer's and the focus session's card (`CountdownTile`) steps its
length with the wheel over it (`CardWheel`), repeats a stepper held down (`CardPress`, `CardDrag`,
`CardRelease`) and lights the button under the pointer (`CardHover`), and its descriptors say
`Interaction.Drag | Interaction.Wheel`.

### Nothing waits for the pointer (2026-10-04)

The person: "right now it does not layout shift when i am in the flyout. this should not be. it
should always update the layout. not holding back when i am there with my mouse." Every flyout
(`FlyoutHost.Fit`: the quick settings' pages, the calendar, the clock, the notifications, the
drives, the weather, the stocks, the contacts, the search box) and every folder
(`FolderFlyout.FolderChanged`) used to hold a shrink while the pointer was on it, until it left.
None does now: what is added, removed, resized or reworded is laid out at once, the pointer on it
or not. The tray's overflow and the app buttons' "…" follow the bar's icons and buttons while they
stand open too (`Dock.FollowOverflow`), where they used to show what they opened with.

What keeps a click honest is that **a press and its release are matched by the thing, not the
place**: the calendar by the target's kind and day (`CalendarFlyout.Same`), the notification list
by the notification or the group (`NotificationsFlyout.KeyOf`), a folder by the widget
(`FolderFlyout.PressedAfter`), the quick settings by the control, which a page keeps between
builds; a thing that went away takes its press with it, and a release on something else clicks
nothing. What still holds, because it has to:

- **A drag under way**: a block carried along the bar keeps the others where they stood while it
  is over one (`DropTargetOf`).
- **A press in the overflows**: "…" and the tray's overflow are not shown again while a button is
  down in them (`Flyout.Pressing`): their rows are numbered by place, and the app has heard its
  icon's button go down; they follow as soon as it comes up.
- **A modal loop**: what arrives while a menu's or a dialog's own loop runs is kept until it
  ends (`Dock.Deferrable`, `Dock.Kept`) — the dock is in the middle of handling something, and
  handling another message inside it would re-enter it.
- **Typing**: a box keeps its caret and its selection through a layout, because a page keeps
  its controls (`QuickPage`) and the notification list its text (`NotificationView`).

### The list folder's shape

Most converted panels become **list folders**, because a panel is a column of things and a list is
a column.

**Which drawing a line takes and how tall the line is are two questions.** A line is the
widget's own drawing (`ListLine.Card`, asked through `Sections.CardInList`) — a **component**'s
card, or a taskbar entry's **list form** (below) — or the folder's row of an icon and a name
(`ListLine.Row`), which is only there for a widget whose click acts: the pin, the switches. How
tall the line is is `Sections.ListRowsOf`, and nothing else reads it.

Tying the two together is a real defect and it shipped: the test was `ListRowsOf(kind) > 1`, so a
component could keep its own drawing **only by claiming two rows**. The day switcher's content is
one line of chrome — ‹ the day's name › — and it came out about twice the height of anything in
it, with a dead band underneath that the user saw straight away. A kind now says both numbers
where they differ (`WidgetSize.ListRows` beside `MinGrid`): the switcher needs two rows in a
**grid**, because below that a card is drawn the way the bar draws it and a component has no bar
drawing, and one row in a **list**, where it has the panel's whole width. Neither number is a
guess about the other. The two partitions happen to coincide across every kind today, so untying
them moved nothing — which is the point: it is a seam, not a change.

`ListRows` is a **floor, not a range**. A component that should be as tall as it needs *within
bounds* is the min/max work, and this is the seam it replaces. **The constraint that work has to
answer:** a folder cannot measure a component. A natural height is a measurement — the day
switcher's answer is "one header line", which is a text metric — and `FolderFlyout.Build` takes no
`Gfx` *by design*: it is a pure layout of the settings and the bar's numbers, which is what lets a
test, a picture and the live panel agree about geometry without a device. So a natural height has
to arrive declared, or be passed in from somewhere that has already measured it. Asking the folder
to ask the widget how tall it is means handing `Build` a device and losing that.

**Every row of a list keeps one set of edges** (`FolderFlyout.RowInset`, `RowIcon`, `RowText`).
One leading icon column, whatever stands in it — a pin's icon, a kind's glyph centred in it, an
app's logo — because the names have to line up. They did not: a pin's icon was 20 and a glyph 16,
each followed by the same inset, so a pin's name began 4 px further in than everything else's; and
a converted panel, laying out its rows on its own numbers, began 14 further in than either. Nobody
wrote those differences down. They are what three places arriving at a layout separately produces,
and the user reads them off a screenshot straight away.

What a list folder looks like is its lists, one setting and one piece of ink:

- **Lists side by side** (2026-10-09: "a list folder holds 1..n lists shown side by side. No
  limit"). A folder is an ordered list of ordered lists (`FolderOptions.Lists`; in the file
  `"lists": [[{ "island": … }, …], …]`, shape 22), each list its widgets top to bottom and the lists
  left to right. **Each list is a panel of its own** (§74, "Lists apart"): its own material,
  corners, rim and shadow, as tall as its own widgets, a flyout's gap (12 DIP, `FolderPlan.ListGap`)
  from the next, the lists lined up on the bar's side; each list as wide as its own preset. A list
  taller than the folder's 70 % of the work area leaves it **leaves out its last lines**, whole ones
  from its end, and the others stay as they are; nothing in the folder scrolls (§152). The reading order the keys walk and a 2×2 face shows is list by list
  (`Folders.ReadingOrder`).
  **Empty lists are kept** (since 2026-10-11, §74 "Empty columns"; it was "no empty list but a
  folder's only one"): a new folder is one empty list, the "+" beside and between the lists adds an
  empty one, and a list whose last widget is removed or carried away stays (`Folders.Take`,
  `Folders.Move`); a list goes only by its own remove, asked first where it has widgets, and never a folder's last
  (`Folders.RemoveList`). A line is carried between lists in edit mode like any line
  (`Folders.Move`, below "Arranging"). The lists share the folder's channels (`FolderIsland` is
  one `IWidgetContainer`), so a month in one list sets the day an agenda in another follows.
- **Width, per list** (since 2026-10-10, §74 "A width per list"): narrow 280, medium 360 — the
  width every panel of an island's content already is, and a list's until somebody chooses — or
  wide 480 DIP (`FolderListWidth`, `FolderOptions.Widths`), chosen beside the list's "+" while the
  folder is arranged. It was one width in DIPs for every list of the folder (`FolderOptions.Width`,
  240–720, on the folder's page); that went.
- **No height to set** (2026-10-09: "folder height = automatic only — remove the folder height
  setting/constraint"). A folder follows what is in it, **while somebody is looking** — growing and
  shrinking at once, the pointer on it or not. A shrink used to wait for the pointer to leave, so
  the lines under the one that went did not come up under it; the person asked for the layout never
  to hold back for the pointer ("it should always update the layout"), and what keeps a click honest
  now is that a press and its release are matched by the widget, not by the place (§9, "Nothing
  waits for the pointer"). The Fixed height that showed what fitted and said what it hid
  ("2 widgets hidden — make the panel taller") went with it; a list that does not fit leaves out its
  last lines, and arranged its warning button says which (§152).
- **No line of the list's own between two widgets** (2026-10-05: "the divider in between widgets
  should in list view should not be there per default, you have to add it deliberately and can also
  move it around then"). The list drew a hairline between every two stacked widgets; it draws none
  now, as the bar draws no separator of its own. Two lines stand the list's own gap apart (2 DIP),
  and a list wears **no card plate at rest**, so what parts two widgets is their own content and
  that gap — unless somebody put a **divider** there (below, "A divider"), the one line a list
  draws between two of its lines. Nothing was stored for the old hairlines, so no file changes:
  a list that had them reads without them, and a divider is in a file only where somebody added one.

### Flyout surface (2026-10-16)

The person: "make sure that the design in terms of colors and shadows and borders is exactly the
same as it is for the native taskbar flyouts." Measured off Windows' own quick settings (Win+A), the
notification center and the calendar (Win+N) on this PC — dark, transparency effects off, 150 % —
captured over the desktop and over a white window:

| | Windows | Karpo's folder before |
|---|---|---|
| body | #242424, solid | #2C2C2C (WinUI's acrylic fallback) |
| rim | 1 DIP (2 px at 150 %), **over what is behind the flyout**: #C8C8C8 over white, #40 over #1C1C1D, #313236 over #04050B — #757575 at 40 % | #33000000 over the body |
| corner | 8 DIP | 8 DIP |
| shadow | none, over white or black (drop shadows on in Windows) | blur 16, 8 down, 28 % dark / 14 % light |
| gap | 12 DIP from the taskbar and the screen's end; 12 DIP between notification center and calendar | 12 DIP (`FlyoutPlacement`) |
| footer | #1C1C1C band under a #191919 hairline (quick settings) | none |

`FlyoutTheme.Taskbar` is that surface for the hosts that are taskbar flyouts (`FlyoutHost.Taskbar`:
folders and quick settings); menus keep `FlyoutTheme.For`'s, the content tokens are the same. Dark
body #242424; light keeps #F9F9F9 (Windows' light flyouts could not be measured here: the PC is in
dark mode and Karpo does not change Windows' settings). The rim is `TaskbarStroke` in both themes and
lies outside the material (`FlyoutTheme.RimOutside`): the plate, the shape that casts the shadow and
the cards' clips (`FolderFlyout.CardClip`) stand the rim's width in (`FlyoutHost.RimInset`), so the
desktop shows through the rim as it does through Windows' — but a graph runs under it to the card's
edge (§185). The shadow only with transparency effects
on (`FlyoutTheme.Casts`), where it is the one it was (that case could not be measured either). A colour
chosen for flyouts stands over the body as before; high contrast keeps the system's colours and a 2 DIP
rim, outside too. Tests: `FlyoutSurfaceTests`.

### List forms

*"No list line without content"*: a line that is the widget's glyph and its name says nothing of
what the widget shows, so a widget with more to say than its name has a line of its own — its
**list form** — and a widget without one is not in a list at all. The list forms:

| widget | its line |
|---|---|
| clock | the time, the date and the zone or label: one row, the date or the place and the time against the trailing gutter; taller, the time over the date and the place, growing with the height, and a face of the time beside them (below, "A line at every height") |
| calendar | an **agenda**: today's page and the events coming in the days the widget looks ahead, filling the line and saying how many more there are; one row, the next event and when it is; shorter than the whole agenda, each event one line |
| battery | the level's glyph, the percentage and what it is doing, the charge as a bar, and the time left in the battery flyout's words; taller, energy saver and the power mode too (below, "A line at every height") |
| brightness | the volume's line with the sun on its button (`SliderLine`): its one slider and the level of the display the folder opened on, however many displays there are; at two rows "Brightness" and the level over the slider, taller the level large (§35) |
| stock | over two rows wherever the height holds two lines of words, a third for the market's state and the holding (§119); before that, its compact line at every height (2026-10-11): the symbol and the company with the price, its currency and the change with its range on a row, the chart at the line's foot no taller than `StockIsland.ChartDip` (60 DIP), a taller line keeping its words at the top and the room between empty — no panel and no accent graph any more; the chart one stroke with round joins; held shorter, the symbol, the price with its currency and the change with its range ("+1.59% 5Y") on a row, or on one row, the chart behind them (§24); a holding's worth on a row of its own or in the company's place (§25.1) |
| now playing | the art, the track and the artist, and its own previous, play or pause and next; one row, the title and play or pause; taller, the transport under the words and the track's timeline between them |
| drive, network drive | the drives flyout's own header: picture, name, kind, the capacity bar, used and free; one row, the name with the bar filling the room after it; taller, how much is free large |
| removable devices | a row per device on the list's edges — its picture, its name, what is free — with "Eject" on the trailing gutter, and the rest said in the last slot; "Nothing plugged in" when nothing is; a row with the room for it gains the device's capacity bar |
| the five graphs | the glyph, the reading's name and its figure, and the graph behind the whole line, faded under the words (§24); taller, the figure large with its detail beside it |
| Security | where the machine stands, who is in charge, the glyph on the accent while it is protected; one row, the antivirus and where the machine stands; taller, both protections, then each with what Windows says of it |
| Windows Update | where the restart stands ("Restart required", "No restart needed") over when (the time Windows scheduled, or the deadline), the arrows in the leading column with Windows' red dot while a restart waits; one row, its name and where the restart stands |
| mail | the unread count over the newest messages, each its sender over its subject, and how many more; one row, the newest message and how much is unread; shorter, a message a line |
| notification list | a list of its own at every height — never the panel's cards, so the line keeps its look as notifications come and go: the bell, the count and "Clear all" over the notifications, each its title over its body where two fit so and else a line each, each opening and its × hiding it, and how many more; one row, the count and "Clear all" |
| pin to a folder, showing its contents | one folder on this PC: its picture, its name and how many items it holds on one row; taller, its items under that, a row each as the drive flyout draws them — the shell's icon, the name, and the date on the trailing gutter where the names keep their room — and how many more in the last slot (§32) |
| screen time | the day's total and the fortnight before it as a graph behind the words; one row, the total; taller, the daily average, then the total large with ‹ › and the graph, a day of which a click shows (§69) |
| app usage | a row per app of the day: its logo, its name over a bar of its share, its time; lit under the pointer, a click opens it; how many more in the last slot (§69) |
| heading | a title over the lines under it: its words in the body's strong weight on the list's gutter, at the foot of one row, with the air over it that sets a group apart, as a group header of Windows' Settings |
| divider | a hairline across the list's whole width, in the middle of a line 13 DIP tall, where somebody put it |

**A folder on this PC** (backlog 14 and 28, consolidated: §32; a widget of its own again since §380,
`FolderContentsLine`, drawn through `FolderContentsView`) was a pin to it set to show its
contents (`PinContents`, drawn by `PinTile`). It was a widget of its own, "Folder contents"
(`fileFolder`), until the person asked for one way to show a folder; a file that still holds one
reads it as that pin. What the folder holds is read off the dock's thread through `FolderSource` —
the drive flyout's order, hidden and system items left out, a hundred listed and the rest counted —
and followed by a watcher, a run of changes read once it has settled (`FolderWatch`). A click on a
file opens it; on a subfolder it does what the pin's navigation says — File Explorer, or its list
beside the row, one level or all levels deep; anywhere else on the card or the line opens the folder
in File Explorer. Its right click is the pin's menu. On a grid: one tile is its picture over the
count, a row or a column of tiles adds its name, and from two by two it is a heading of the folder
over a row an item. One that is empty or not allowed says that; a folder this PC does not have is a
broken pin. `FolderReadingTests` and `FolderPinContentsTests` hold it over made-up folders.

**A heading** (backlog 29, `HeadingTile`, a list's alone, `heading`): a title over the lines under
it, one level — it heads the lines down to the next heading. Its words are its settings
(`HeadingOptions.Text`, one line of at most 60 characters); one nobody named says "Heading" in the
language Karpo speaks, in the same ink, and asks for nothing — no "Set up in Settings" (2026-10-11:
"the heading should not show a setup button but should have a default value shown";
`WidgetSetup.Needs` has no heading). It does nothing when clicked and never lights under the pointer
(`FolderFlyout.Quiet`): the air over it is what sets its group apart, as in Settings.
**Its own height** (2026-10-11: "the heading should not have a configurable size, it does not even
have to conform to the 1cell height, it can have its own size actually"): a section heading's, not a
row's — 8 DIP of air, BodyStrong's 20 DIP line (14 DIP semibold, grown with the text scale), 4 DIP
under it (`HeadingTile.Height`, 32 DIP at a text scale of 1), laid out by `FolderFlyout.Build` as the
divider's gap is, so edit mode's places and drops follow. It has no height card in Settings
(`ListKind.HasHeight`); a height a file still holds for one is dropped as it is read, nothing else
touched. `ListLineLookTests.AHeadingHasItsOwnHeight`; pictures `HeadingPictures`.

**A divider** (2026-10-05, `DividerTile`, a list's alone, `divider`): a line across the list between
the line over it and the line under it, **put there on purpose**. The list draws no line of its own
(above), so this is the only way a line comes to stand between two widgets.
- *Added deliberately*: "Divider", under Folders with the heading, in a list folder's add list (a
  "+" of the folder), lands where that "+" was, as every line added from the list does; the bar's
  list has none. No other add puts one in, but a ready-made list group comes with its own
  between its groups of lines (§7b, "Ready-made groups", "Its dividers"), each moved and removed as any.
- *Moved as any line*: in edit mode it is carried to another place in its list or another list of
  the folder (a drop lands it through `Folders.Move`), selected by a click, which opens its
  page, and removed with its menu's Remove. Dragged out onto the bar it is refused, as a
  heading is: the bar has its own separator.
- *A split, not a line* (since 2026-10-09, §78): it splits its list's panel into two cards, the gap
  Appearance's "Dividers" say apart (6 DIP by default), whatever its range says; it draws nothing
  and edit mode draws it as a rule across its gap (§121). It never lights, and a click on it does nothing.
  It has no height to choose in Settings (`ListKind.HasHeight`), and its right click at rest is
  "Settings" alone.
- `ListFolderTests` (no line of the list's own; a divider splits the list where it was put),
  `DividerStyleTests`, `AddListTests.AListsDividerIsAddedOnPurposeAndMoves`, `ListLineLookTests`; in
  pictures, `folder-listedge-*.png`, `list-headings-*.png` and the gutter sheets.

The keyboard, the desktops, the layout switcher, the date and the bell have none: they are the
taskbar's alone (2026-09-26), and a line of theirs would be a glyph and a name. The volume
slider's line is the sound panel's volume row (`soundVolume`, "Volume" in the list's library): a
slider carried into a list becomes that row. The brightness's line is the same line (2026-10-11,
the person: "the volume and brigness slider look different in terms of layout, this should not
be"): both ask `SliderLine.Lay` where the button, the slider, the level's field, what it sets and the
large level go at a height — the flyout's row on one row, the button, what it sets and the level
over the slider on two, the level large taller — and place the quick settings' own `Button`,
`Slider` and `Label` there; both are their kind's row tall (`VolumeLineTests`, `slider-lines-*.png`
side by side). The timer's and the focus time's lines are their
cards on the list's own edges (`CountdownPlace.Line`), each with its own countdown and name.

**One drawing per subject.** A list form is drawn by the class that draws the widget's card, on
its `WidgetSurface.List` branch, from the pieces its card and its flyout already paint — never a
second drawing of the same thing. Where the flyout has a region that *is* the line — a drive's
header, a stock's header — the line re-houses it whole, laid out by the flyout's own layout at the
list's width and filled by the same code the flyout fills it with (`DriveHeader.Show`,
`StockHeader.Show`), placed so its own gutter lands on the list's (below, "One gutter"). The rest
are laid out on the list's own edges (`ListForm`): the glyph or picture in the leading column, the
first row of text where every row's name begins, anything more under it in the same column — so a
form one row tall is exactly a row of the list. The calendar's page is one drawing on its card and
its line (`CalendarIsland.Page`), with the agenda beside it on a line, or under it where large text
leaves the page no room beside the events.

**How tall.** Each form reports its content's own height (`IListContent`), measured with nothing
summarised, and the line is given exactly that inside its range. A form's line measurement starts
at one row and ends where the content stops having more to show — for one whose content is one
fixed thing, the rows that hold it at 225 % text, measured, which `ListFormTests` holds at both
sizes. The agenda is a list that grows, so its most is the panel's own and past it the agenda
fills the line and says how many more there are (`WidgetFill`), as a component's list does. A
line is its drawing at whatever height it is set to and is cut at its edge, as a component's card
is (`CellIsland.PaintOn`) — except that the lines below ("A line at every height") are drawn for
the height they are given, and never cut.

**A click does what a click in a folder may** (§15): nothing that opens a popup. The clock, the
calendar, the battery, a stock, a drive and what is playing are lines whose click does
nothing (`ListWidget.Act`), so what they would open on the bar stays shut; a graph and Security are
lines that act — Task Manager and Windows Security open, because an app opening is what a folder
allows; and what is playing's buttons are its own controls, each its own target, handled there
with the folder left open.

**A pair of numbers, read where the widget stands.** A subject with a taskbar entry and a list
line has a width on the bar and a height on its line (`BarKind.HasSize`, `ListKind.CardInList`),
each the pair of the widget that stands there (§12.3): the settings show it as a Width on the bar
and a Height in a list. Carried from the bar or a grid into a list it becomes its line
(`Partners`) and starts over, as one made straight into a list does: at its line's measurement
(`ListKind.New`), not at its width on the bar.

### A line at every height

*"the grid ones have been optimized very well for all the different sizes. for the list view
widgets they have not been optimized ad all. they should also be optimized to look good from 1 to
6 cell heights (maybe even higher depending on the type of widget). they should keep their
functionality for every size if possible."* A line was one drawing: given less than it measured
it was cut at its edge, given more it left the rest empty. The readings' lines — the five graphs,
the battery, a drive and a network drive, removable devices, the weather now and a stock — and the
clock's, Security's, the calendar's, mail's and the notification list's are drawn for every height
from one row to their most (`ListWidget.Range`, one to six rows at least), the way a grid card is
for every span (§16):

- **One row is one line of the list**: the glyph in the leading column, the name where every name
  begins, the main reading against the trailing gutter, a sparkline or a bar between them where
  there is room for one (`ListTiers.LeastPicture`), and at most one control — the weather's
  refresh, a device's Eject. The clock's reading is the time, with the date or the place it stands
  for as its name; Security's where the machine stands, with the antivirus's name; the calendar's
  when the next event is, with what it is; mail's how much is unread, with the newest message; the
  notification list's name is how many there are, and "Clear all" its control.
- **The compact line**, from two rows, adds the second readings and a compact graph or bar: a
  graph's peak, the memory in use, down and up, read and write; what the battery is doing and the
  time left; how much a drive has free; a stock's company, and its day under it; the date under
  the time; who is in charge under where the machine stands, and both protections under that;
  today's page beside the events; and the events, the messages and the notifications one line
  each.
- **The whole widget** fills the height from where it fits — at the list's text three rows for a
  graph, the battery and a drive, four for the weather and five for a stock: a graph's figure large
  with its detail beside it — in use and available, down and up, read and write, the peak and the
  average — and the history in the rest; the battery's energy saver and power mode; a drive's kind
  and how much is used; the weather's header, the next hours and the days ahead; a stock's header
  and its session from bell to bell; the clock's time larger and a face of it, from three rows;
  each of Security's protections with what Windows says of it; and an event, a message or a
  notification in two lines — its title or its sender over when it is, its subject or its body —
  from where two of them fit so. What is shorter than the line stands in the middle of its height.
  A glyph grows with the tier, 16 to 20 to 24 DIP (`ListTiers.GlyphPx`), into the room before the
  text and never into the gutter (`ListTiers.GlyphBox`).
- **Past six rows** a line with items shows more of them, not bigger type. Removable devices share
  the height up to two of the list's rows a device, and a device's row with the room for it gains
  its capacity bar and what is free under it; a line shorter than its devices shows what fits and
  says how many more (`WidgetFill`). The agenda, the inbox and the notification list do the same
  with their events, messages and notifications.

**The tier is what fits, not the number of rows** (`ListTiers.Of`): the fullest whose pieces fit
the height at the text size in force, so a line one row tall at the largest text is one row, and
three rows at 225 % text are one row's line in the middle of them. The whole widget's figure grows
modestly with the height, 26 to 36 DIP, and where the rest leaves it less room it is as large as
fits and never smaller than the compact line's (`ListTiers.FullValuePx`). **A taller line never
says less than a shorter one:** where the whole widget's larger figure would leave out a line the
compact line shows — the time left, a graph's peak — the figure gives way, or the line stays the
compact one. A line of items shows no more of them a line each than the whole widget shows in two
lines where it starts (`LineRows.Items`), and the calendar's page grows only where it stands beside
the events, so the events keep their room. A line as tall as its own content — where a new one
starts, and where an Automatic one stays — is rarely a whole number of rows, and draws the tier it
was measured for.

**The reading wins.** On one row the reading's field stands against the trailing gutter and the
name takes what is left (`ListTiers.Row`): its full name, else its short one — "Processor" then
"CPU", "Zürich, Switzerland" then "Zürich", "SANDISK (E:)" then "E:" — else cut with an ellipsis
while its first four letters still show, else none: a name cut to a letter or two says nothing
(`ListTiers.Name`). What gives way next is each kind's own: a stock's change before its symbol, so
two shares' lines still tell apart; a drive's free figure before its name, because the name and
the bar filling the room after it are the line; what the battery is doing goes under the bar
rather than being cut beside the figure. Half a detail is never drawn: a graph's detail beside its
figure shows whole or not at all.

**A line keeps what it does at every height.** The weather's refresh stands on the trailing gutter
from one row up, each shown device keeps its Eject, and a graph's line opens Task Manager wherever
it is clicked. The notification list's "Clear all" is there from one row up, and each notification
it shows opens, and hides by its ×, at every height; Security's line opens Windows Security
wherever it is clicked. What a short line leaves out — the devices past the ones its height shows,
and their Eject; on one row, the notifications themselves — belongs in the kind's right-click
menu.

`ListLineReadingsTests` draws each of these kinds at every height from one row to its most, at
100, 150 and 200 % and at 100 and 225 % text: nothing it draws leaves its line, none of its words
or glyphs overlaps another, and one row tall it still says its reading. It holds the shared
pieces on their own, and pictures every height of each kind side by side at 150 % to
`list-<kind>.png` in `%TEMP%` (`KARPO_LISTS_DIR` where set). `ListLinesTests` holds the clock,
Security, the calendar, mail and the notification list the same way, laid out through a sketch that
says what it drew (`LineSketch`, `ILinePieces`), at heights half-way between rows as well: every
piece inside its line and its gutters, none on another, the reading on one row, the tier a line
was measured for at its own height, never fewer items on a taller line, and the compact
notification list's × and "Clear all" hiding what they should. Its sheets go to the same place.

**The controls' lines are drawn the same way:**

- **A switch** — its glyph, in the accent while it is on, its name, and on the trailing gutter the
  switch itself where a click switches what it stands for (`IQuickSwitch.Switches`), else its state
