  in words; then what it is doing and what a click does under the name; then the state large with
  the switch beside it. It is drawn from the switch's own data, so a switch added to the list has
  its line with nothing of its own.
- **A pin** — its icon with the running indicator under it and its name; then whether it is open
  and what it opens; then the name large, a pin's name being its reading.
- **Now playing** — the art, the title and play or pause on one row; the art beside the title and
  the artist with previous, play or pause and next; with the height, the transport under the words
  and then the track's timeline between them, which a press seeks and a drag scrubs, the open
  folder ticking the line a second while it shows one; in a narrow list it keeps three buttons,
  shuffle and repeat left to its menu, and where even that does not fit a taller line is the compact
  one — never a centred column (2026-10-11). Where it plays — the app's icon, or the favicon of the site
  a browser plays it on — stands in the list's leading column at every height (the note where none was
  found), naming it under the pointer, and the whole widget names it under the
  artist (`NowPlayingSource`; a browser's site that stands in the artist's place is said once).
  The art is on the right and the words on the left at every height and on the face (2026-10-11, the
  person: "show the album art on the right and the text on the left"): the art holds the trailing
  gutter, an icon's column on one row, with the transport before it; the words start on the leading
  gutter and are cut before it; a track without art keeps the slot, the note in it. On the face
  neither is centred: the words start on the face's leading end and the art ends it, a short track
  too (the person, later the same day: "right now they are centered which i dont want")
  (`MediaPresetTests.TheLinesArtIsRightOfItsWords`, `TheFacesArtIsRightOfItsWords`, `MediaRowTests`).
- **The apps playing** (`mediaSources`, 2026-10-11: "the now playing folder should show the
  selector for the source again. where i can choose brave or spotify") — the media flyout's
  "Playing in" list as a line: a row per app with a session, its icon, its name and whether it
  plays, the one followed ticked in the accent at the row's end. A click follows that app. The
  pick is the dock's one (`MediaPick`): every now-playing line, face and list follows it, never
  written down. The media preset is now the line, the apps playing and the volume, no output
  device; folders made before keep their lines (`MediaPresetTests.TheSourcesPickWhatTheLineFollows`).
- **The volume** — the flyout's own row; then the output it sets over the slider; then the level
  large between them. **The sound lists** — the device in use, or one app's level, on one row;
  then their rows, drawn closer before any is left out, with the heading over them where it costs
  no row; a mixer too short for all its apps shows the person's own before Windows' sounds.

`ListLinesControlsTests` holds them as the readings are held, and pictures them the same way.

What their short lines leave out is in their right-click menu (`Dock.WidgetMenus.cs`): now playing's
previous and next, and for its timeline where the track stands ("2:03 of 4:32") over a step back and
a step on through it; every output device and every microphone under its name, the one in use
ticked, a pick making it Windows' default; and every app's mute, the person's own apps first, ticked
while muted. `ListMenuCoverageTests` reads each from a real line and does it through the line's own
controls.

### One gutter

*"the widgets for weather and other stuff in the list view dont have the proper spacings on the
side"*: each line had kept the gutter of the place it came from — the weather's header and a
drive's the panel's 16, a day of the week its row's 8, screen time's 20, the sound page's 8 and 20,
a stock's day its prices' width — so a folder of them started its words at five different places.

**Every line of a list stands on one gutter: the list's own row inset** (`FolderFlyout.RowInset`,
asked through `ListForm.Gutter`), 12 DIP at 100 % text and growing with the text as the list's rows
do. Not the panels' 16: the list's own rows (a pin, a switch) and the list forms already stood on
the row inset, it is the one air the list keeps since the folder's own pad went (§9, "The list
folder's shape"), and it scales with the icon column and the names it sits beside. The lines that
moved are the ones re-housing a panel's region.

- **Whatever a line draws at rest stands between its two gutters**, and what leads or ends it stands
  on them: the first letter, a right-aligned figure, the list's icon column, a meter's end, a card's
  or a chosen row's plate, a button's box. A button's glyph sits in the middle of its box, and a
  device's icon inside its plate, as far in as they do in the flyout.
- **A panel's region keeps its own gutter inside itself and is placed so it lands on the list's**
  (`ListForm.Housed`): the weather's header and its days, a stock's header, a drive's header.
  Moved, never redrawn. Screen time lays its plan out on the list's gutter (the ring and the week)
  or as much narrower as puts the day switcher's arrows on it; the sound lines put their headings on
  it and their rows between; the notifications' cards stand on it.
- **A graph is the one thing that crosses it.** A line whose picture is a graph — the five readings,
  a stock's chart, the day's temperatures — runs the graph edge to edge across the whole line, with
  nothing behind it but its own fill: no plate, no band. The five readings' and a stock's are the
  line's ground, behind its words and faded under them (§24). Its words stay on the gutter: the
  reading's name and figure on it, a stock's header, and the hours, glyphs and values a day's
  graph writes, each centred on its own hour and left unwritten where it would reach past the gutter
  (`DayGraph.Gutter`) rather than pulled in beside its neighbour. A stock's day is its session, bell
  to bell, so the price starts at the line's edge; the weather kept its night shaded to the edges,
  because when it is dark is information, not a ground — till §572 took the shaded night and the sun's
  hairlines off the weather's graph: nothing stands behind its line now.

`ListGutterTests` draws every kind a list holds at 100 % and 150 % and at the largest text, and
reads each line back a row of pixels at a time: nothing but a graph inks the gutters, a graph
reaches the line's edges, and the words lead and end on the gutter.

### Filling the room

> **Superseded for lines of items (2026-10-11, §109).** The person: *"if content is cut off by the
> fixed height the widgets should always be scrollable in list view. dont just show x more items,
> let the user scroll down to see all of the other items too."* A line of items given less than its
> items take now scrolls inside itself (`ListScroll.cs`); no list line says "N more" any longer.
> What follows is kept as the record of the rule it replaced. `WidgetFill` survives only as the
> whole-items arithmetic (`summary` 0) and a folder pin's contents, whose rest is the folder it opens.

**A component shows what fits and says what it left out; nothing inside a folder scrolls.**

That is the rule, and it is general — every kind, not a habit some of them have. A card of a
folder is the room the component was given: it lays out as many whole items as that room holds and
**spends its last slot on a summary of the rest** — "12 other apps", "and 5 more" — rather than a
pager or a scrollbar. Where there is nothing sensible to summarise, showing fewer items is the
fallback; a scrollbar is not. A component never grows in place either: growing changes the
folder's geometry and can strand its neighbours, and the folder's geometry staying still while you
look at it is the invariant everything else depends on. Growing is a resize, which is the user's
own act.

This replaced a paging control, which was a correct answer to the question as it stood and was
answered differently: *"the contents should try to fill all of the space. if there is not enough
space for an item dont show it or try to work around it... dont make the stuff scrollable."*

**Built** (`Karpo.Dock\Islands\WidgetFill.cs`): `WidgetFill.Of(count, item, summary, room)` for
rows of one height, `Of(items, summary, room)` for rows that differ, `Rows(room, item, chrome)`
for a component whose own builder summarises from a row count, and `Says(left, shown, one, many)`
for the wording. It answers `Shown`, `Left`, `Summarised` and `Height`. Three things make it
honest rather than nearly right:

- **The summary is a real row.** It is measured with the others and takes a slot of its own, so
  the arithmetic can never end with a summary drawn in room that was already spent — which is the
  failure every hand-rolled version of this has.
- **Room for exactly everything shows everything**, with no summary at all, and a summary never
  stands for a single item: the item fits in the slot the summary would have taken and is better
  in every way.
- **One wording.** `Says` gives "12 other apps" where some are shown and "12 apps" where the room
  held none — "other" with nothing above it reads as a mistake — so two components cannot describe
  the same situation two ways.

A summary row is **a statement, not a control**: nothing leads anywhere from it, because the
folder is already showing everything it has to say. That is also why a converted component's
`Interaction` is `Click` and not `Wheel` — a component that does not scroll has no claim on the
wheel, and leaving it claimed stops the folder under it scrolling for nothing.

The **order** is the component's only contribution: screen time summarises the smallest shares and
notifications the oldest arrivals, which is one rule ("summarise the tail as ordered") reached for
different reasons. A mechanism that summarised by some idea of importance would have to be told
what importance means per kind.

**The folder itself never scrolls** (§152, 2026-10-12): a list taller than 70 % of the work area
leaves out its last lines, as the bar leaves out the widgets it has no room for.

### Arranging

A folder opened by a click is **read-only**. The steppers, the
remove badges and the wobble live behind an explicit act — the
bar's edit mode, or a Customise affordance in the panel. Otherwise every click on
a widget becomes an invitation to dismantle it, and someone drags the graph out of
their screen time by accident with no idea what happened.

**A drag is that act** (2026-10-05: "when a widget is dragged in the grid or list view it should
also automatically switch into edit mode"). A card or a line carried past the drag threshold in a
folder at rest turns the bar's edit mode on, and the folder is arranged where it stands without
closing, the same card carried on (`FolderFlyout.HandOver`; §7, "A drag at rest turns edit mode
on"). A click stays a click, and a slider's drag stays the slider's. What makes it no accident is
what the bar's own hand-over shows: the edit bars and the settings app come up with edit mode, so a drag nobody meant is
plain to see and one Escape away. Before this a drag at rest carried the widget out of the folder
and onto the bar with no edit mode at all, and a release inside the folder did nothing.

**One folder at a time, in edit mode too** (`OneFolder`, 2026-10-09: "in edit mode as in normal
mode, only one folder can be open at a time"). Opening a folder closes the one open, as its own
button would, so nothing it held is lost. At rest a folder is a popup like any other. While its bar
is arranged it does **not** close on a click elsewhere — it stands through the drags and presses on
the bar behind it — and closes only on its own button clicked again, another folder opening,
Escape, or edit mode ending. The edit mode's pair of folders side by side (`FolderPair`,
2026-09-26), which carrying a widget from one folder into another needed, is gone with it: a line
moves inside its folder, between its lists.

**The "+" buttons, and nothing moves** (2026-10-09: list spacing "must be identical in edit and
view mode"). Arranging a folder changes none of its layout — the same panels, the same lines in
the same places at the same size, the same title (`FolderFlyout.Build`,
`ListFolderTests.ArrangingAFolderMovesNothing`) — and adds round "+" buttons, every one the same
Windows accent button (`FolderFlyout.PaintAdd`, 24 DIP), each opening the add list and the widget
picked landing where the button was (`FolderAdd`, `FolderPlace`):
- **at each list's own end away from the bar, outside its panel**, following that list's height:
  over it on a bottom bar, where the widget goes at the list's top; under it on a top bar, where it
  goes at the list's end;
- *(gone 2026-10-12, §148: the empty slots out to the screen's edges have their own "+")* **in
  every gap between two lists, and outside the outer two**: a new list there, level with the
  middle of what the panels either side have in common. The gap is 12 DIP and the button 24, so it
  lies a little over the two panels' edges. An empty folder has only its list's own "+": a new list
  beside an empty one would be that list.
- **none between two widgets** (§74): a widget goes in between two others by a drag.

What stands outside the panels stands in the room the window keeps round them while the folder is
arranged (`FlyoutHost.OutsideDip`, 36 DIP on every side but the bar's; the panels stay where they
were), drawn over everything (`FlyoutHost.Outside`). Where that room or the display has no space —
a folder against the work area's edge, the bar's side of a side bar — the button comes in over the
folder's edge, as little as it takes (`FolderFlyout.KeepIn`). A line carried onto a "+" for a new
list is a new list there.

**Carrying a line** in an arranged folder lands it where the pointer is: in the list it is over or
nearest — across the gaps between panels and the room over a shorter one too, which are still the
folder for a drag — above the first line whose middle is below the pointer, else at that list's
end — an accent bar across the list on that seam shows it (`FolderFlyout.MarkFor`) — or, over a "+"
for a new list, in a new list there. Where letting go would change nothing (just above or below itself, or a new
list beside the list it is alone in), nothing is shown and the release is a click
(`FolderFlyout.Ghost`, held to `Folders.Move` by `FolderModelTests`). Let go, the list it left goes
where that was its last line.

**A folder opens under a carried widget, and only that one** (`BarCarry`, the person: "multiple
folders open because even though you are already in the folder area it somehow still moves the
widget down at the taskbar as well"). A widget carried along the bar in edit mode that rests on a
closed folder's button for 700 ms opens it, so it can be put in a place of its choosing. The rest
counts from a move of the pointer on the button: a button the bar's own blocks slid under a pointer
standing still is not one the person went to. Over an open folder's panel — its panel, not the
shadow's room around it, which on the bar's side reaches down to the bar (`FolderFlyout.Offer`, as
`Flyout.OnPanel` for the tray's overflow) — the folder has the widget, and the bar stands as it did
when the pointer left it: the gap and the carried block stay where they were, nothing lights, and no
folder button below the pointer is rested on. The bar holds the mouse through the drag, and it used
to go on reading the pointer's x as a place along it there: it put the gap at its very start,
sliding its blocks along under the folder, and rested the widget on whichever folder button stood
below the pointer, which opened a second folder. Back on the bar, the drag goes on from where it was.


## 10. Nothing managed crosses to WinRT

The bar ships as one native AOT executable (`scripts/publish.ps1`). One rule falls out of
that, and it binds every widget, every surface and every service the dock runs:

> **A managed collection cannot be handed to a WinRT call.** No `string[]`, no `List<string>`,
> no collection expression, no LINQ result. Pass `null`, or pass a collection that came from
> WinRT in the first place.

The WinRT parameter is an `IIterable<T>`, and handing it a managed object asks the runtime to
build a COM wrapper for that object on the spot. Under the JIT it builds one. Under native AOT
the wrapper has to have been generated at build time, and for these types nothing is generated —
the CsWinRT AOT source generator emits **no files at all** for this project, which you can see
for yourself by building with `-p:EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles=true` and looking in
`obj/…/generated`. So the call throws before it does anything:

```
InvalidCastException: Failed to create a CCW for object of type 'System.String[]'
for interface with IID 'E2FCC7C1-3BFC-5A0B-B2B0-72E769D1CB7E' (HResult 0x80004002)
```

This cost a user-visible bug: the Bluetooth flyout said "no devices" on a PC with a headset
connected, because `DeviceInformation.CreateWatcher(aqs, additionalProperties, kind)` threw on
its property list and the failure was swallowed. Two things came out of fixing it, and both are
the standing advice:

- **Say it in the query, not in a property list.** Where an API takes a filter *and* a list of
  properties, the filter can usually carry the same fact. The Bluetooth watcher now runs one
  query per answer — paired and connected, paired and not, and so on — so *which* query found a
  device says what the property would have said. See `Karpo.Dock/QuickSettings/Services/Bluetooth.cs`,
  whose header is the long version of this section.
- **Where the query cannot, go native.** Two facts have no filter to hide behind — what kind of
  thing a device is, and its battery percentage — so both are read from the device's own PnP
  nodes through SetupAPI instead of WinRT
  (`Karpo.Dock/QuickSettings/Services/BluetoothNodes.cs`). P/Invoke has no ABI edge to fall off,
  and one walk costs 0.42 ms a device, 3.4 ms for eight, measured on a background thread.

**No test can catch this.** Tests run under the JIT, where the wrapper is built on demand and
every one of these calls succeeds; the failure exists only in the published executable. The
guard is instead `Karpo.exe --smoke`, which `scripts/publish.ps1` runs on every publish and which
exercises the real services once against the real machine, and `Karpo.Core/Troubles.cs`, which
writes what failed — type, message and `HResult` — to `karpo.log` beside the config. A `catch`
around a WinRT call that reports nothing is how this stayed invisible for as long as it did.

## 11. A widget's constructor makes the object; the first look starts the work

**Since 2026-09-27 this is the drawing's rule and not the data's.** The person: *"widgets like the
processor display / graph only get initialized when i open the folder. they should get initialized
on start so that they can already show the accumulated historical data. this should go for all
widgets"*. A widget is its data and its drawing, and they were one object, so the lazy rule below
held the data back with the drawing: a graph in a folder began its history when the folder opened,
a weather card in a closed folder was fetched once at the start and never again, and a widget in a
layout no display shows gathered nothing at all.

The data is a **source**'s now (`Karpo.Dock\Sources`, `DataSources`): one per kind of data — a
reading, a place's forecast, a share's price, the calendars and inboxes of the accounts,
the notifications, the sound devices, what is playing, Windows' security state, one switch, the
volume — made at the dock's start for every widget the config names, on any bar, in any folder,
in any layout, shown or not, and gathered at its own interval, unchanged. Every widget of a kind
of data reads the one source: sixteen processor graphs are one reading of the processor and one
history (`PerformanceData`, where the history lives now), sixteen hotspot buttons are one switch.
The config holds a source while it names a widget of it (the dock asks after every change of the
config) and a widget holds its source while it lives; the last hold stops it. The dock's timer
ticks the sources whether or not a bar is on screen, and a widget that ticks asks its own source
first, which reads once an interval however many ask.

The drawing keeps the rule below: nothing is drawn that nobody sees, a closed folder's widgets
are not ticked, and a drawing expensive only while drawn stays lazy. What a store already shared
(weather, stocks, calendar, mail, notifications, sound, media) is kept running from the start by
its source and read by the widgets as before; the calendar and the media sessions go on for the
dock's life once started, as they did once a widget had asked, because the clock's panel and the
quick settings read them too. Some kinds need no source: the battery and the drives are read in
one call when the widget is made, the calendar's taskbar entry is the date (its card and its line
are the ones that show events), and the contacts button draws no contact — its panel reads the
address books when it opens (below). An isolated run — every test, every `--smoke` pass — reads no
notification of the person's, as it reaches no account.

Making a widget must not ask Windows anything. Whatever it has to find out — a radio, a
connection, a device, a file — is started the first time somebody **looks** at it: drawn on the
bar, drawn as a folder's card, hovered for a tooltip, clicked. And what is started must not
block, because for a widget on the bar the first draw is the first frame, so the asking goes to
the pool and the answer comes back through the widget's own redraw.

The one-button widgets are where this was learned. `SwitchIsland`'s constructor called
`IQuickSwitch.Start`, and the mobile hotspot's start is two live network-stack queries —
**60 ms the first time in a process, 8–11 ms warm**, measured. A bar with that widget paid it
while drawing, at every start.

**The reason this is a rule and not a note about one widget** is the folder. `FolderIsland`'s
constructor calls its own `Configure`, which builds every widget in the folder — so a hotspot
sitting in a folder **nobody ever opened** paid the whole cost at startup, invisibly, because a
closed folder's widgets are never drawn and so never appear in anything measuring paint. A
folder cannot hold a folder (all three folder kinds declare `Tile = WidgetSource.None`), so this
is one level deep, not recursive; but it is as wide as the folder has cells, and converting a
panel to a folder (§9) is exactly the act of making it wide.

That constructor is not the thing to change. A folder's size is a function of its cells (§4,
§8), so it needs its widgets in order to measure itself, and making it lazy would mean a second
"measure without making" path in every kind — a lot of machinery one level above where the
problem lives. Keep the rule in the widgets and the folder is harmless however wide it gets.

What a widget shows before its answer arrives: **blank, never wrong.** No state at all rather
than a state it guessed — and no explanation either. The hotspot's tooltip used to say Windows
would not let Karpo share this connection whenever it had no manager, which during the gap meant
it said so while it simply had not looked yet. A wrong explanation is worse than no explanation.
State arriving must not change the widget's size, which §4's rule already gives: a shape is a
function of its options and the metrics, never of what it currently says.

**The second widget to learn this was the calendar, and it sharpened the rule rather than
repeating it.** Its events come from the person's accounts, and a first look is a request to
their mail provider with their own sign-in — a cost no other widget's first look has. The
temptation was to make the panel the only door, but a bar widget that says "open the calendar to
see your events" is a widget refusing to do its job; the answer is the same as the switches' —
first draw — plus a failure that rests before the next try, so a widget redrawn through a hover
asks once and not sixty times. The mail widget, which draws its unread count, follows it exactly;
the contacts button draws no contact and waits for its panel. What changed is where the guarantee
lives. It is not in the widget and not in each drawing path, because a drawn widget is exactly
what `--smoke` and the offscreen pictures produce: it is in the stores, whose accounts
(`AccountSet.Shared`) are the person's only when `Config.IsIsolated` is false. An isolated run —
every test, every smoke pass — gets a set with no account in it, so a new caller of `Open` cannot
get this wrong (`docs\accounts.md`).

The switches were moved to that shape afterwards, and they turned out to need it. The guarantee
there had been each caller remembering to hand over a made-up switch, and `KARPO_QUICK_SAMPLES` —
the flag the smoke sets while saying in the same line that it reads no radio — reaches the
flyout's pages and never reached these, so the smoke's own airplane and hotspot widgets were
enumerating this PC's radios and querying its live network stack. `QuickSwitches.For` now gives
an isolated run switches with nothing to reach, and where the smoke wants Windows' own exercised
natively it builds them itself and says so. **When the first look costs the person a decision and
not just a millisecond, put the guarantee in the thing being reached, not in the things reaching
for it.**

Going the other way is just as much a rule. **A read is allowed to stay on the drawing thread
when caching it would make it wrong** — `HotspotSwitch.On` asks Windows every time, at 223 µs a
read, because there is no state-changed event to hoist it onto and a cached answer would sit
stale after somebody toggled the hotspot in Windows' own Settings. The dock has no render loop,
so that cost is per redraw, not per frame. Measure before hoisting, and say in the code why
something that looks expensive is staying where it is.

## 12. How big a widget is

The four rules here were worked out against the person's own bar over a run of complaints —
"little widgets should be 1 by 1", "the weather widget is just huge", "by switching states the
widgets should not change the layout", "when there is no possibility to make it look good
vertically then flip the contents". They lived in a working note for a while, which was a
mistake: the note was never in the repository, so a dozen comments pointed at a file nobody could
open. They are here now, and the code points here.

### 12.1 The grid: one cell is the bar's own square

A **cell** is a square whose side is the bar's usable thickness — the height somebody chose, less
the breathing space above and below the highlights (`Layout.BaseCellDip`, 2 DIP each side). A
widget is one cell across and a **whole number of cells** along. Nothing on the bar is a fraction
of a cell, except the one thing that is not in cells at all (below).

That is what makes a click, a highlight and a drawn surface all land on the same square, and it is
why a widget on a taller bar grows rather than floating in a bigger box: the cell grew with the
bar. A little widget is 1 by 1 because a glyph in a square is a glyph in a square at every height.

**Inside a widget, its own cells need not be squares.** A widget made of pieces of its own lengths
(`WidgetShape.Row`) is rounded up to whole cells once, and its last pieces keep their own widths
while its first has the rest. The now-playing widget was the first of them, its three transport
buttons compact at its end; the taskbar entry has no buttons now (§12.5) and is one piece. A click,
a highlight and a surface still land on the same rectangle, because all three read the one set of
lengths (`IslandCells.Exact`, which the layout takes as they are).

The **separator** is outside the grid (`WidgetSize.InCells`), not an exception inside it. It is a
line, and its footprint along the bar is the line's own thickness and nothing else: on an islands
bar it stands in one ordinary gap between its neighbours with the line centred in it, and on a
connected bar, which has no gaps, it sits flush between them (`Layout.Between`). It used to be
`OneCell`, and that cell was real — a range whose ends meet is a chosen width, so every separator
took a whole square of bar with a line drawn in the middle of it. How thick the line is
(`LineStyle.Width`, in hairlines, so it lands on whole pixels at every scale) and how much room it
keeps either side of it are Appearance's, the same for every separator (§78), and in edit mode it can be taken hold of
`SeparatorGrabDip` either side of its block, ahead of the widgets beside it
(`Layout.SeparatorUnder`), because a line a pixel wide is not something a pointer can find.

**Space either side** (2026-10-06: *"the separator should have the configuration option of space
on the sides so that it can visually separate everything"*). `LineStyle.Space` is DIPs of
room on each side of the line, rounded to whole pixels where it is laid out (`Layout.LineSpace`),
and held to `MaxSpace` (48). It is the separator's own: its block along the bar is the line and the
space twice, the line drawn in the middle of it (`Layout.LineRect`, which `Scene` draws), and the
gap it stands in is shared out around the line as before (`Layout.LineSide` reads the line alone),
so the space adds to what the bar already kept there, the same on both sides, in every look and on
every edge. Edit mode's block, its ring when selected and its grab zone hold the space.

**Any number, not only steps** (2026-10-08: the line's width and the space *"fully customizable"*).
Settings gives each a slider with a number field beside it (`EndsSlider`, then a `NumberBox`),
any whole number: the line 0 to 8 (`LineStyle.MaxWidth`), where 0 is Automatic and the field
is then empty and says so, and the space 0 to 48 DIP (`MaxSpace`). Since §78 these are on
Appearance's "Separators", one style for every separator; a separator's own (`"separator": {…}` on
the item) is dropped as the file is read. The line stays
in hairlines (one at 100 %, two at 200 %), which the field shows as px: a width in DIPs would put a
"1" half on a pixel at 150 %.

A list folder's divider (`DividerTile`) has the same three settings, its own on Appearance's
"Dividers" (§78): a line or none, its width, and the room over and under it.

The **tray's icons** stand in cells of their own size along the bar, as Windows' tray does: a cell
is a square twice its 16-DIP icon, 32 by 32 DIP, centred across the bar (§33, §38). The tray widget is as long as
its icons, never rounded up to whole cells (`BarKind.Tray` has no size of its own, `HasSize`).

### 12.2 A widget's size follows its settings, never its state

**For a folder's faces on the bar this is superseded by §244** (2026-10-19): a face is as wide as
what it shows now. Every other kind keeps the rule below.

Already the rule in §4, and stated again here because the failure has a distinct shape when it is
about *size*: a widget whose size follows what it currently says will resize as the world changes
under it, and the bar will jump. The notifications widget changed width when a notification
arrived; a drives widget was measured from the drive it happened to be showing.

So a size is measured from the **settings object**, not the live widget (`WidgetShapes`), and a
kind that shows a reading reserves its worst case — the widest string that reading can ever be —
rather than the one it has. The temperature widget reserves `-88°` in Celsius and `188°` in
Fahrenheit, per unit, because the worst case is not the same on both scales. The scale is
Localization's, not the widget's (§37), so a scale chosen there, or a region changed in Windows,
re-measures every weather widget alike.

There is a class of bug hiding behind this rule and it is worth naming: a widget only follows its
settings if it is **given** them again when they change. Thirteen kinds never refreshed the
settings object in `Configure`, so a folder switched to show its name kept the square it was born
with. `SettingsFollowTests` holds that generically — every kind, handed a different settings
object, must measure what the new settings say.

### 12.3 The range: what it may be given, and what it works out to

**Down a list this is superseded by §76** (2026-10-09): a folder widget's height is Automatic up to
a most or Fixed, not a least and a most; what is said here of a list line's range is history. Its
rows are one to the kind's most, and no kind has a fewest of its own (2026-10-13, §166).

**On the taskbar the range is the kind's, and nobody sets it** (2026-10-08, §12.6). What follows is
the rule as it stands for a list line's height, where the person's two numbers are still the whole
answer, and for the layout, which holds every part to the range it is handed.

Three quantities, and only two are ever stored.

- The **range** is the person's: the fewest cells a widget may be given and the most
  (`Island.AtLeast`, `Island.AtMost`), each 1 to 32 (`Island.MostCells`), the most never below the
  fewest. Both are always written, as numbers.
- The **natural size** is what the content works out to. It is not stored and nobody types it,
  because it is a measurement of the content, taken fresh every time it is needed.
- The kind's **measurement** (`WidgetSize.MinCells`, `MaxCells`, `DefaultCells`) is only where a new
  widget's range starts (`WidgetBounds.DefaultFor`). It is not stored with the widget and caps
  nothing a person chooses.

The whole rule is one line, and it is `WidgetBounds`:

```
given = bounds.Clamp(natural)
```

**What is given is what is drawn.** The layout measures and places a widget with its range, and
the scene draws it with the same range (`Layout.StyleFor`). The scene used to be handed only a
width somebody had pinned, so a range that still decided the size — a minimum over the natural
size, a maximum under it — gave a widget a slot of one length and drew it at another: the
now-playing widget painted its natural width into a slot a third larger, its words cut to a few
letters and the rest of the slot blank. `MediaRowTests` holds every cell's surface to its slot.

**The person's two numbers are the whole answer.** In their words: "there should not be an
automatic selection. it should be min can be from 1 to lets say 32 or so and max can be from 1 to
32, and max has to be bigger or equals to min. the region between min and max is where the
automatic size is applied." So the size card is two dropdowns, Minimum and Maximum, each 1 to 32
and nothing else (`SizeRange`, `SizeCard`). Between the two the content decides; the same number
in both is one fixed size — "a range it can grow and shrink in, or one very specific size" is one
setting, not two. The end just picked wins and the other moves only to meet it; in a file whose
ends disagree the fewest wins, because a minimum is a promise about being readable and a maximum
is only a preference about room.

That reverses two rules that stood here, both at the person's asking.

- **A preference was clamped into a measurement.** A person could narrow what a kind could do and
  not widen it, so a clock set to twenty cells was given eight and a one-cell kind had no size to
  choose at all. Not any more: a clock set to twenty is twenty, and a Wi-Fi button given three
  cells has its glyph in the middle of three. A range stopped being a lie the moment nothing
  narrowed it, which is why every kind in cells has the card now, the one-cell kinds included.
- **Nothing was written until it was chosen.** A widget nobody had sized carried no numbers, the
  card said "Automatic", and a handful of rules read that silence as a meaning of its own. Now a
  new widget is made with both ends written where its kind starts, a file's own tidy writes any end
  that is missing, and what the card shows is what the file holds.

The maximum is why this is a clamp and not a starting point. **A widget already at its maximum
must not be handed one more cell because a cell happened to be going** — a maximum a spare cell
can overrule is not a maximum. That still answers "the weather widget is just huge": a new widget
starts inside what its kind measures, so a media widget with a long title shortens at eight cells
instead of running to ten, until somebody gives it more.

Some things keep a size of their own kind, and `Sections.HasSize` is the list of who has the card:

- The **separator** is a line, and its size is the line's thickness in hairlines and the room it
  keeps either side (§12.1).

- The **tray**'s size is how many icons it shows, and **show desktop** is a sliver at the bar's
  end rather than a cell.

Twelve kinds draw one glyph and have no branch anywhere that reads more room, so they say
`WidgetSize.OneCell`, and one cell is where they start. That number is a **measurement, not a house
style**: the test is whether the drawing has a branch that uses the room, not whether a wider one
would look odd. Given more, the glyph stands in the middle of it.

A widget that cannot be given its minimum is **dropped rather than squeezed**, and the bar says
nothing about it: a badge on a bar already too crowded to hold its widgets is the last thing that
bar needs. It records what it dropped (`Layout.NotShown`) and the edit rail does the telling,
where the person is already doing the thing that would fix it. A minimum of 32 cells on a small
screen is a widget the bar drops; that is the person's to see in the rail, not the bar's to overrule.

**Down a list, the same rule.** A list folder's line is `clamp(natural, bounds)` of height, where
the bounds are the person's least and most in rows of the folder's cells, 1 to 32 as a width is
(`WidgetBounds.For(island, WidgetType.List)`), and the natural height is the content's own. Three
things are particular to it.

- **The content is measured by the widget, and handed to the plan.** `FolderFlyout.Build` takes no
  device, on purpose — it is what lets a test, a picture and the live panel agree about geometry
  without one — so it cannot measure a component. The open folder can: it asks each component
  through the one seam there is (`IListContent.ListHeight`) and passes the answers in. A line
  nothing measured is what its kind declares (`ListRowsOf`), which is exactly the height it had
  before ranges existed.
- **A new line starts at one row.** On the bar the range and the content cannot disagree about
  rounding, because a widget's content is already whole cells. In a list they can: content is in
  pixels and the range is in rows, so a least of two rows would round a 48 px band up to a 77 px
  line — the empty room under the Today card, rebuilt. So where a new line starts is one row to its
  kind's most (`WidgetBounds.DefaultFor`), and its content is its own floor, never less than one
  line of the list, until somebody picks a least.
- **Every component has a height to choose, and its kind says where it starts.** The kind's list
  measurement (`WidgetSize.ListRange`) is the most a new line starts with: for a list of
  notifications, apps, devices or days, the rows the panel it came from stood at; for a card whose
  content is one fixed thing — the day switcher's band, the week's graph, today's curve — enough
  rows to hold it at the largest text Windows offers, because rows follow the display's scale and
  not the text's. Anything that is not a component draws the list's own one-line row and has no
  card at all.

One pair of numbers is a height down a list; along the bar there is none to set (§12.6). A widget
in a list for its click is the list's one-line row there, and its numbers mean nothing while it
stands there. A taskbar entry with a list form (§9, "List forms") has its pair as a line and none as
an entry: carried from one surface to the other it starts over at the size a new one starts at
there (`Partners.Convert`), the room its kind gives on the bar and its line's measurement in a list.
`SizeRangeTests.NoTaskbarEntryHasTheCard` and `EveryLineWithAHeightGetsTheCard` hold which have one.

While the folder is open a line follows its content under the panel's own rule: growing and
shrinking at once, the pointer on it or not, whether the panel's own height is Automatic or not.

### 12.4 Vertical: four branches, in this order

A bar standing on the left or right edge has a cell as wide as the bar is thick, and most widgets
have more to say than fits across it. A widget takes the **first** of these that works, and never
a later one while an earlier one would do:

1. It fits as it is.
2. It **stacks** what it says onto rows — a time's parts, a label's words, a glyph over its value —
   and **steps the text size down**, within what stays readable.
3. It **says less**: the day's number without the month, "Mo" for "Mon", no change row under a price.
4. It **drops the text** and keeps the widget.

Text is never rotated (the person, 2026-10-13: "if possible dont try to flip text"); the turned
clock that was branch 3 is gone (§162).

Say less before saying it smaller, and step a size down before cutting a word: **a label somebody
chose is never shortened, only stepped down.** A widget is never dropped by this rule — branch 4
leaves the glyph, which is the widget still being there.

The measuring for it is `VerticalFit`, and the one thing to watch is what "the room across" means:
it is the cell less the widget's own edges on both sides, not the cell. Getting that wrong gives
every vertical widget a little more room than it has and the error only shows at the narrowest
bars.

### 12.5 A taskbar entry is one row

The user: *"also make sure that the taskbar widgets layouts are designed to take up one row only"*.

Across a horizontal bar every taskbar entry is **one row of content**, in the middle of the bar, at
every height from the thinnest to the tallest. A thick bar used to buy a second row: a glyph over
its value, a symbol over its price, the weekday over the day, a drive's name over its capacity bar,
a graph under its reading, the clock's time over its label, the weather's condition under the
temperature, the input language over its region. Content that wants height is a grid or a list
widget's now. On the bar, each entry's row is designed rather than being what was left of two:

| entry | its row |
|---|---|
| clock | the time, then "· label" or what its own timer or focus session has left |
| calendar | the day and the date, as the date entry had them: the date joined the calendar (2026-09-27), and the calendar's badge and next event left the bar |
| weather | glyph and temperature (the condition after them came only at a chosen width, and there is none now, §12.6) |
| stock | symbol, price, change, on the day's chart faded behind them (§24) |
| now playing | the title over the artist, then the art (on the right since 2026-10-11), the artist quieter, where two lines fit (below); else "title · artist" on one line, where both do not fit the title keeping three fifths. No transport buttons: they are the card's, the list line's, the flyout's and the right-click menu's |
| drive | icon, name, then the capacity bar from one gap after the name to the widget's end; the bar keeps its least length before the name has any, and the name shows wherever the letter fits in the rest; no free-space figure, which is the tooltip's, the flyout's and the list line's |
| performance | glyph and reading, on the graph: the graph is the entry's ground, its whole width and height, faded under the row (§24); room the widget is given past its row lengthens the graph's unfaded stretch |
| battery | glyph and value side by side |
| brightness | the sun and its one slider, the volume slider's own plan at its defaults (the two are one family and share their size); the sun alone, quiet, where the slider has no display to set (§35) |
| timer, focus time | the glyph, its name where it was given one ("Tea"), and the length set ("5m"), or what is left, always five figures ("04:59", "01:05" from an hour up); over, its name in the figures' place where the entry has no room for both |
| input indicator | one cell, square where its codes fit one, wider where not: "ENG" over "CH" where two lines fit, else "ENG", at 11 DIP, under the clock and a step under Windows' indicator's 12 (2026-10-11, "make the ENG CH text on the keyboard face smaller"; below, §61) |

**Two entries with two lines: now playing and the input indicator.** The person (2026-10-08): the title and the artist on
two lines where the bar is tall enough for two lines at a readable size, else one. Two lines of the
entry's own text size (`Fit.Primary`, never shrunk to make them fit) must fit across the cell with
a sliver of air above and below — the rule the taskbar's clock went by for its time over its date —
which is a bar of 40 DIP or more at 100 % text; a thinner bar or larger text keeps the one line
(`MediaIsland.TwoLines`, measured on a template, so the lines never come and go with the track).
The two lines are one block in the middle of the bar, each cut with an ellipsis on its own, and they
take the same column the one line does, so the entry is as wide either way. The same day the
entry lost its previous, play or pause and next: it is the art and the words, one piece, centred,
and a click opens the media flyout. `MediaRowTests` and `MediaSizeTests` hold both; `OneRowTests`
holds every other entry to one row and the now-playing one wherever two lines do not fit.

The input indicator, the same day: *"the keyboard layout widget on the taskbar shows on two rows
where possible (e.g. "ENG" over "CH", as Windows does), in a 1×1 cell (square, like an icon)"*. It is
one cell, whatever it shows (`WidgetShapes.Keyboard`), and in it the language over the region, one
block in the middle, where two lines of the bar's text size fit the cell's height with a sliver of
air (`KeyboardIsland.Room`, `TwoLinesFit`). A thinner bar has the language alone, as Windows'
indicator has on a taskbar of small buttons. Since 2026-10-09 the codes are never shrunk to fit the
square: the cell is wider than square where they need it (§61). A layout with no region is its language alone in the same cell. Down a vertical bar it is as
it was, the region under the language. `KeyboardSquareTests` holds it, and its sheets
(`keyboard-square-<dpi>-<look>.png`).

**One size per row.** Where a row has several pieces of text they share one size, so they share a
baseline. The hierarchy a second line's smaller size used to carry is carried by ink and weight:
the quieter ink, a semibold symbol, the weekday in the accent.

**The text still grows with the bar.** One row on a tall bar is set larger, not left at 12 DIP in a
band of air: it is the cell's share (`Layout.CellTextDips`, 12 DIP on the taskbar's 48 DIP bar,
capped at 32), as it always was. The glyph beside it grows with the cell (§12.1), and a pair whose
glyph grew while its text did not stops reading as a pair. The cap keeps a very tall bar a taskbar.

**What it costs.** A stack used to save a cell, and a row does not: the battery is two cells on the
48 DIP bar where it was one. The input indicator is one again, its stack being Windows' own. Widths follow from
`WidgetShapes`, which still measures templates and never content, so nothing moves as the content
changes.

**Down a vertical bar the stacks stay.** A line across a narrow vertical bar often has no room
("Wed 28.12." in 48 px), so there the glyph stands over the value, the weekday over the day, and so
on, under §12.4's branches. It is the one place a taskbar entry stacks, and the code says so where it
does it (`CellPair`, `GlyphAndText.Stack`, `DateIsland.Stacked`, `DriveRows.Stacked`, `Fit.Leading`).

`Karpo.Tests\Sizing\OneRowTests` holds all of it twice. On the drawing: every line of text, glyph and
shape of its own an entry draws shares one band. In the pixels: sheets at 28, 36, 48, 72 and 128
DIP, dark and light, where each entry's ink is one unbroken band, its text one line tall, in the
middle of the bar.

### 12.6 A taskbar entry has no size to set (2026-10-08)

The person: *"remove the ability to resize widgets on the taskbar. taskbar entries take the size they
need"*, and with it no layout shift.

- **No setting.** "Width on the taskbar" (`SizeCard` on a taskbar entry's page and on a folder's)
  is gone, and its strings with it. The card is a list line's height and nothing else (`SizeRange`),
  and a grid card keeps its span (`SpanCard`).
- **No numbers in the file.** A taskbar entry has no size of its own (`BarItem.HasSize` is false):
  none is written, and one a file still holds — "atLeast", "atMost", the tray's too — is dropped
  where the file is read (`BarItem.Normalize`), without a word, and is not written back. A folder's
  widgets keep theirs, but for a pin: **Start and pins have no width anywhere** (the person: "no
  configurable width for the Start button and pins"). Start stands in no folder; a pin's card in a
  grid has its span and carries no numbers, one a file still gives it dropped where it is read
  (`CellItem.Normalize`); a pin's line in a list keeps its height, one row to six.
- **The room is the kind's.** The bar lays an entry out in its kind's range
  (`WidgetBounds.For(BarItem)` is `WidgetBounds.DefaultFor(kind)`), which is where every entry used
  to start, so a bar nobody had resized looks as it did: a drive is its two cells, a one-glyph
  button one, anything else as wide as its content works out to, up to its most. Edit mode had no
  handles for a width, so nothing there went.
- **Still, as its value changes.** A width somebody chose was what held a few entries still, so each
  is still on its own now: every entry drawn by a widget class is sized from its settings and
  templates (`WidgetShapes`), and two that were not are now. The clock on the bar keeps room for
  the widest its time reads in its format, evening and morning (`Scene.WidestTime`,
  `Clock.Widths`), so ten o'clock and noon no longer move it; what follows the time — a label, or
  what a timer somebody started has left, always five figures — is its settings and that timer.
  A share keeps one room for every price across the bar, four figures to the cent
  (`StockIsland.PriceRoom`), where it used to be measured on the price it had, so a price arriving
  or crossing 1,000 moved the bar. The status icons, the open apps and the tray are as many as there
  are, as on Windows' taskbar. `EntryWidthTests` holds all of it.
- **What went with the chosen width.** Three things were only ever shown at a width somebody chose:
  the weather's condition after its temperature (the weather's *Detailed* look is its replacement, §12.7), the year in the calendar's date, and a volume or
  brightness slider longer than its own. On the bar they no longer show; the flyouts have them.

### 12.7 Looks: a taskbar entry drawn in more than one way (2026-10-09)

**Gone with the weather entry (2026-10-09, §80).** The weather was the one kind with looks; it is
the weather preset now, and its three looks are the weather face's *Look* option (`WeatherFace`,
`WeatherFaceDrawing`). `BarEntry.Looks`, `BarLook`, `WeatherLooks`, `BarItem.Look` and the Settings
row (`LookRow`) went with it, and their words. A face's options are what a look was meant to
become: what "eventually other widgets too" asks for is a face with options (§67). What follows is
the record as it stood.

The person: *"the weather widget on the taskbar should get different layouts, you should be able to
configure the look in the settings … eventually I want to add this to other widgets too."* So a
**look** is generic, and the weather is its first user.

- **The mechanism.** A kind lists its looks in its registry entry (`BarEntry.Looks`, each a `BarLook`
  of an id; the first is the default). The entry's choice is `BarItem.Look`, an id in the
  file: absent is the default, and the default is never written; a word this build does not know is
  kept as it is and read as the default (`BarItem.LookId`); a kind without a choice drops it
  (`BarItem.Normalize`). The words are keyed `core.look.<widget id>.<look id>.title` and `.blurb`.
- **Settings.** The page of an entry whose kind has more than one look shows a **Look** dropdown
  (`LookRow`, the card in `WidgetsPage.xaml` shown by `IslandOptions.HasLooks`), its description the
  chosen look's blurb. No kind appears in that code: a kind that lists looks gets the card.
- **To give another kind looks:** list them in its `BarEntries` entry; add the title and blurb of each
  in the five languages; have the kind's shape (`WidgetShapes`) and its island's painting read
  `BarItem.LookId`, from one plan so the size and the drawing cannot disagree (`WeatherRow`).
- **The weather's looks** (`WeatherLooks`, `WeatherBarLooks.cs`), each one row at every height and
  as wide as its content, from templates and never from the forecast (§12.2):
  - *Simple* (default): the conditions' glyph and the temperature, as it always was.
  - *Detailed*: the same and today's high and low after them, in the quiet ink, in one box so a
    figure changing moves nothing.
  - *3-day forecast*: today and the next two days — the region's short weekday (`Nls.ShortDayName`,
    the widest of the seven is the room), the glyph, and "18°/8°", the high loud and "/8°" quiet, from
    the start of a box as wide as the widest pair. Starts at the place's own today, so a forecast that
    is hours or days old never shows a day gone. (First drawn with the high and the low each
    right-aligned in a box of its own: twelve evenly spaced pieces, "18°   8°   Sat", in which the days
    could not be told apart. As one pair the room a short pair leaves falls between the days.)
  An hourly look was left out: one row of time, glyph and figure for four hours is as wide as the
  forecast and wider than a thin bar can carry, and the flyout has the hours.
  Down a bar on its side, and before a place is set, the weather is the simple look whichever is
  chosen. The weather's range now goes up to the most (as the clock's does), since three days are
  wider than the old eight cells. Tests: `BarLooksTests`, `WeatherLooksTests`, and `OneRowTests`
  holds every look of every kind.

## 13. Three sections, each laid out on its own (2026-10-05)

The bar had been one ordered list whose growing spacers pushed its runs of widgets apart. The
person's trouble with it was that widgets whose size changes — app buttons coming and going, a label
changing, the tray growing — moved everything, the middle included. So the bar is **three sections**
again, and spacers are gone (from the model, the layout, edit mode, the settings app and the add
list; the house rule "every bar keeps a spacer" is withdrawn):

- the **start** (`BarSection.Start`), aligned to the bar's start: the left, or the top on a bar
  standing on a side;
- the **middle**, centred on the bar;
- the **end**, aligned to the bar's end: the right, or the bottom.

**Each section lays out on its own** (`Layout.Positions`, `Layout.SectionStarts`). A size change in
one section only rearranges that section: the start's widgets run from the bar's start, the end's to
its end, and the middle's are centred on the bar whatever the other two hold. When they run out of
room, in this order:

1. the middle stays **exactly centred** as long as that keeps it a widgets' gap clear of the start
   and the end;
2. then it **moves as little as needed** not to overlap them;
3. then the app buttons fold into "…" as before (`FitTiles`);
4. then the old rules: islands give way, the last placed first (`NotShown`, which the edit rail
   lists); past that the sections run one after the other from the bar's start and the tail falls
   off the end.

**The model: one list, a section on every entry.** A layout keeps its one `islands` list, and every
entry carries `"section": "start" | "middle" | "end"`, always written (`BarItem.Section`). The list is
kept in its sections' order — the start's entries, then the middle's, then the end's
(`Sections.Order`, run by `Config.Repair` and by every edit) — so a place on the bar is a section and
an index in the list (`BarSlot`): the end of one section and the start of the next are the same
index, and the section says which is meant. One list rather than three because everything that
reads the bar — the three-way merge entry by entry (`ConfigMerge`), a widget's id, pin sync, the
folders — reads one list, and a widget moved to another section is then one value changed. With
three lists the merge would read the move as an entry taken out of one list and put into another,
and a removal wins over the other app's edit of it (`SectionFilesTests`).

**Places along the edges (2026-10-07, chunk A of the places plan).** Every entry carries
`"edge": "bottom" | "top" | "left" | "right"` (`BarItem.Edge`), always written: it stands along that
edge of the screen, in its section there, **the same on every display that shows its layout**. (Since
§41, 2026-10-08, the places a layout's widgets stand in are those of its type — a Taskbar's three on
its edge, a Dock's middle, a Top and bottom's six — and how each bar shows is the layout's; what
follows on Position and "None" is how it stood before.) A
display's Position (`Screen.Edge`) only says which edge is its fixed bar — always in sight, holding
its space — and the other three edges' sections are places shown when the pointer reaches them; it
never moves a widget (the person, 2026-10-07: "the same layout can look different on different
screens ... it should not change the location of the widgets itself, it should just change the
appearance of the row of widgets"). The bar shows its edge's entries and nothing else
(`Sections.Along`, `Dock.Shows`). Position "None" (`"fixed": false` on its `Screen`, written only
then) makes every edge places. The list is kept by place — the bottom's entries, then the top's, the
left's and the right's, each by its sections (`Sections.Order`); `BarPlace` is an edge and a section,
and `Sections.Range`/`Put` take one. An older file's entries had no edge and stood on the bar of
whichever display showed them: `Config.Repair` gives each the edge of the display that shows its
layout (`Config.EdgeFor`: of displays on different edges, the primary's; with none, the bottom) and
writes it, so the shape stays 17; an edge in a word this build does not know is given one the same
way. (Since shape 19 an entry has no edge: it stands in one of its layout's six slots, a row and a
section — see the named layouts below.) A new entry nobody placed is in the main row
(`Sections.Insert`), and a layout whose type does not show that slot gives it a shown one
(`TaskbarLayout.Home`); the settings app's add, the layout's (`PlacesTests`).

**The places' windows (chunk B).** Every place that has something in it and can come in has a
`DockWindow` of its own (`DockWindow.Place`; `HoverPlaces.Wanted`), made at each arrange and kept
while it stays; an empty place, or one on an inner edge, has none. A place is no appbar and holds no
room: it stands in its stretch of the edge (`HoverPlaces.Area`; its third until §45, which shares the
edge by what each place holds), floating whatever look the bar wears,
acrylic where the bar is clear (`HoverPlaces.Dressed`), out of sight with only its 1 px strip
(`HoverPlace.Strip`) taking the mouse. The pointer on the strip slides it in, over every other
topmost window, and with it every other filled place on that edge (2026-10-07: "when going to one
side it should show all the 3 locations"); they settle together as an auto-hidden bar does, staying
while the pointer is on any of them or a flyout, menu or preview of one is open, and going once
nothing holds any of them (`EdgeReveal`); never while a full screen app is in front, the left button is held, edit mode is on or the
demo runs. Shown, it takes the mouse on its panels and the room under them only — each place brought
in with its edge takes its panels at once (`IEdgeWindow.Show` sets the region too: a window's region
clips what it shows, so a sibling left with its strip came in unseen, and the person saw each third
come out alone, 2026-10-07). A peek for an app that wants attention brings in the whole edge too. A place out of
sight is built when it next comes in, not with every change. A display with no bar keeps an anchor
window instead: a strip of nothing, no clicks, there to hear of full screen apps, which it passes to
the display's places as the bar does (`HoverWindowsTests`, `HoverPlaceSheets`).

**Edit mode across the places (chunk C).** Edit mode is every display's at once, or none (2026-10-07,
round 3: "all displays are in edit mode together"): on each, the bar (or, with no
bar, the anchor, which holds the keys and shows nothing) and a window for **every** place along its
edges (`HoverPlaces.Wanted` with `editing`), all in sight at once — a filled place with its widgets,
an empty one as its empty room (`Layout.EmptyRooms`), every section that cannot show all it holds with its small edit bar
beside it (§7, "Where the adds are"). A place on an edge another display touches is a place like any
other while the display is edited (2026-10-07: "inner edges can be filled in edit mode: drops are
allowed. They just can't hover-open at rest"): it takes what is dropped on it and added to it, and
at rest it has no window and nothing waits on its edge, so what it holds shows only in edit mode.
While all are in sight the sides stop a corner short of the top and the bottom
(`HoverPlaces.Clear`), so no two corner places stand on each other. A place's bar is its one section
from end to end (`Layout.Only`). The bar the edit mode was begun on has the keys. A window's parts are not
the list's own — the list holds every edge, the bar shows its own edge's, a place its own section —
so every drop, add, file drop and widget out of a folder goes into the list by the entry beside it,
in that entry's place (`IslandEdits.ToList`, `DockWindow.ListSlot`; `AddSpot.To`/`Edge`). A folder
made, or ungrouped, in a place stays in it (`PlaceEditTests`, `EditPlaceSheets`).

**Carrying a widget in edit mode** (the person, 2026-10-07). A drag that starts in a place carries
into edit mode as one on the bar does, and then:

- *The widget follows the mouse*, anywhere on the screen: the bar a drag began on lifts the block
  and keeps it out of sight, and a window of its own (`EditCarry`, Dock.EditCarry.cs; topmost, no
  activation, no pointer) shows it at the pointer, held where it was taken hold of — the very
  visuals, through a visual surface of the lifted block (`Scene.Carried`).
- *There is always somewhere to land*: the surface of the display nearest the pointer — its bar and
  the room between it and the screen's edge (`DockWindow.DropArea`, `EditDrops.Nearest`; the one the
  block came from keeps a tie) — and in it the nearest place along it (`Layout.DropSlot`), however
  far off the pointer is. A folder standing open under the pointer has it first, as before.
- *The others slide to make room*: the surface it would land on lays itself out again with the
  widget in (`Layout.Carry`, `Layout.Landing`, measured as it was where it came from) and its parts
  glide apart to open the room it will take; on its own bar the gap opens as ever
  (`Layout.Arrange`). The bar it was carried away from closes up behind it (`Layout.Closed`, a
  section it was alone in an empty room again).
- *The drop location is a blue ghost of the right size*: the widget's block where it would land, at
  its size there, in the target's wash and accent ring (`Scene.ShowGhost`, `EditView.Offered`,
  `EditView.Away`), gliding with the parts beside it. Let go, it lands there.

`EditDropsTests`, `EmptyRoomSceneTests` (the scene's empty blocks, the ghost, a bar closing up), and
the pictures `edit-places-{bottom,none}[-drag]-dark-150.png`, `edit-places-{top,left,right}-dark-150.png`,
`edit-places-bottom-light-150.png` and `edit-places-bottom-dark-100.png`; every one, and
`TheFixedBarStandsInsideTheSmallScreenAtItsEdge` on each edge, checks the bar's panel lies inside the
small screen, flush with its edge, and that the bar, the places, the edit bar and the labels stand
clear of each other.

**Where edit mode stands** (the person, 2026-10-08: "edit mode doesn't shrink the screen any more";
§44). The small screen, its wallpaper copy, the frame round it and the motion that zoomed into it
(2026-10-07, round 4 and after) are gone: every display is dimmed (`EditShade`, 40 % black, as
before round 4), and its layout's bars are edited where they stand at rest — a bar shown all the
time along its edge, a bar on hover brought in, every place of it in its stretch of the edge, the
empty ones with their empty room. Edit mode comes and goes at once. A click on the dim leaves edit
mode on and clears the selection, Ctrl or Shift held keeps it (`EditClicks.OnFrame`); a drag on it
selects (§42); no click anywhere ends edit mode. The displays' edit bars and the sections' edit bars
stand in front of the dim on every display (`EditStack`).

**Edit mode and the settings app** (the person, 2026-10-07). Entering edit mode gives the keys to
the bar being edited and opens nothing (round 6, §43: it opened the settings app before); while edit
mode is on a settings window that is open, or opened by the edit bar's "Open settings", stands over
every other window, and it is an ordinary window again when edit mode ends, however it ends. Its side menu's **"Edit"** switch
is gone since §42: edit mode's own "Open settings" and "Close edit mode", beside "Add a widget", are
the way to the app and out. The two processes talk through a registered message, `karpo.editing`,
beside `karpo.edit` (Dock.EditSettings.cs, Karpo.Settings' KarpoProcess, SingleInstance and
MainWindow.Edit.cs): the dock posts 1 or 0 to the settings app's listening window as edit mode
begins and ends, and the app sends 1 to ask whether it is on — what a settings window that starts
while edit mode is on reads.

**One line in Task Manager** (the person, 2026-10-07: "put them all under the same group just
Karpo"). Task Manager folds a process into its parent's line only when both run a file of the same
name; measured on Windows 11 (26200), a shared AppUserModelID, the same file description or a shared
job object leave a windowed child on a line of its own. So the settings app's file is `Karpo.exe`
too, in its `settings` folder (`AssemblyName`), and the dock starts it as its child, with
`KARPO_DOCK` set to the dock's process id. A start the dock didn't make (the Start menu, Explorer, a
pin) is handed to the running dock before WinUI starts: WM_COPYDATA to a bar with the arguments, the
dock answers at once and starts the app again from its queue, and the first process ends
(Karpo.Core's SettingsHandOff, Karpo.Settings' DockHandOff, `SettingsApp.Handed`). With no dock, or
an older one that doesn't answer, the start goes on as before. A trial window (`--new-window`), a
test's (`--test`), one on a config of its own (`KARPO_CONFIG_DIR`) or one set up by a
`KARPO_SETTINGS_*` variable is never handed over. The dock and the settings app now tell each other
apart by path, not by name: the dock's `Focus` and `Find` pass over the dock's
own file, and the settings app's `KarpoProcess.Find` over its own.

**Old files load whole.** A file that still holds spacers is not converted faithfully — the
person's own is reset — but nothing is lost and nothing throws: its runs between growing spacers
become its sections (one run the start; two the start and the end; more the start, the middle for
every run between, and the end), every entry is written with its section, and the spacers, growing
or fixed, go (`ConfigWords`). An entry with no section, or a word this build does not know, is the
start's.

**The default bar is Windows 11's** (`Sections.DefaultLayout`, §23.5): the weather (where Windows shows
its Widgets button) at the left; Start, search, Task view, the pins and the open apps in the middle;
the tray, the status icons, the input indicator, network, sound, battery, the calendar, the clock,
notifications and show desktop at the right. Where the person's own Windows taskbar is left-aligned
(§23.5), Windows' buttons stand at the left and the weather before the tray, as Windows moves them. A widget added later still goes where its kind belongs (`SectionOf`): Windows'
buttons in the middle.

**Where a drop lands** (`Layout.DropSlot`, `Layout.SectionAt`). In the section under the pointer —
between two sections the nearer one, so the room between them is half each side's — at the nearest
gap among that section's own parts: before the first whose middle is past the pointer, else after
its last. An empty section's place is its empty room while the bar is arranged and, at rest, the point it
would grow from: the bar's start, its centre, its end — so files dragged to the middle of a bar with
nothing in the middle make the middle's first pin. The pointer, not the carried block's middle,
decides, so both ends of every section are reachable at any width (`DropSlotTests`).

**What files over the bar show** (2026-10-04: "the blue area that appears should have the size 1x1
or what the new pins size would be"). Files, folders or an app dragged from File Explorer or Start
over a bar at rest show the **new pin's own cell**, in the target's wash and ring, at the size the
pin will have — one app button — and at the very place it will land, its section opening the room
it will take as it does for a carried block (`Layout.Landing`, `Scene.Drag`, `EditView.Landing`):
the start's and the end's widgets move along, the middle grows about the centre, and the other two
sections do not move. It is worked out by laying the bar out again with the pin in it
(`Layout.WithNewPin`), once per place the pointer reaches. Where the bar would not show the pin, the
line between the parts says where it goes, as before. `DropLandingTests`, and the pictures
`drop-landing-{start-end,middle-first,middle-between,end-first}-*.png`.

**No hatching** (2026-10-07: "remove the hatching"). The stripes that crawled over the bar's free
room in edit mode from 2026-10-05 are gone; an empty section shows as an empty block instead (§7).

**Between sections, by mouse and by key.** A block carried over another section goes into it, and
the section it left closes up (`Layout.Arrange`); Ctrl+arrow past a section's end carries a widget
into the next section, an empty one included (`IslandEdits.Step`). The keys and Narrator walk the bar
left to right, top to bottom: the start's blocks, the middle's, the end's (`EditStops`,
`BarUia.Entries`), and then the sections' edit bars. The room around and between the sections, an empty section's place and the grip
band are the bar, where its own menu opens (`Dock.PlaceOf`).

**Windows' Start** no longer follows anything: Karpo does not place it (2026-10-08, §26).

Pictures: `sections-{bottom,left}-{rest,edit}-{0,4,30}-*.png` (the default bar with real widgets, no
app open, four and thirty, at rest and in edit mode, across the bottom and down the left), and the
add-button and drop-landing sheets. `SectionLayoutTests`, `AddButtonProbeTests` (two thousand bars).

## 14. Which popup has the screen

Karpo's popups are three kinds, and the kind decides both what a press does to
them and whether another may open over them (`LightDismiss`, `PopupRole`):

| Role | Opened by | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| `Menu` | a right click | context menus, jump lists, a block's options, the Start button's quick links |
| `Flyout` | a click | an island's list, the tray's hidden icons, a pin group's members, the calendar, the notification list, quick settings, a folder |
| `Hover` | the pointer resting | the window list, the desktop flyout, the media controls |

**A hover popup never opens over one that already has the screen**, as on the
taskbar. `WidgetHover.Pointer` arms its timer only where nothing else is open;
with something open, the pointer coming to rest does nothing at all. Only the
*first* open is refused — once hover's own popup is up, moving to the next
widget swaps it at once, because that is the same popup moving rather than a
second one over somebody else's.

**What counts as open is `Dock.AnyPopupOpen`, and it is three things, not one.**
The dock's generic list is one popup among several, so asking `FlyoutOpen` alone
saw only that one and let the desktop flyout open on top of the calendar:

- `FlyoutOpen` — the dock's own generic list.
- `FlyoutHost.OpenMenus` — every open `Menu`-mode host, on this bar or another.
- `editor is not null` — a bar being arranged, where a folder stands open
  through every press and nothing at all should open by hovering while somebody works.

**Only a `Menu` host is counted, and that is the same rule seen from its other
side.** A host joins the open list, and takes the mouse hook with it, only in
`FlyoutMode.Menu`; `Hover` and `Tool` hosts never do. The edit rail is a `Tool`
host for exactly that reason — a `Menu` host is light-dismissed by a press on
Karpo's own bar, which is the one press the rail has to survive — and it needs
no exception here, because edit mode already stands the hover popups down
through `editor`.

**A hover popup never takes the press that closes it.** `LightDismiss.Consumes`
answers false for `Hover` whatever the button and wherever the press landed: the
window list goes, and that same click still switches, activates or launches. A
`Menu` takes it only on what opened it (§129; it took every press until 2026-10-11,
so going from one widget's menu to the next took two right clicks). A `Flyout` takes it only on a left or middle press on
what opened it, so a second click on the clock closes the calendar instead of
reopening it, while a right click there still opens the clock's own menu.

## 15. A widget in a folder cannot be clicked

In the user's words:

> "as a rule i want you to enforce. generally a widget cannot be clicked in any folder view.
> with this i mean that no flyout should open when the widget is clicked. this also means that
> any widget that does not display contents on itself where it does not make sense to even show
> it in the folder should not be showable in the folder"

Two rules, and the second follows from the first.

### 15.1 In any folder, a click on a widget opens no popup

Grid and list alike. A popup is anything that opens over the screen and waits to be
dismissed: one of Karpo's flyouts (the calendar, a quick-settings page, the drives, the
generic list of items a widget hands over) **or one of Windows' own** — Start, Search, the
widgets board, the touch keyboard. From inside a folder any of those is a popup
opening out of a popup, which is the thing the rule is against.

What still happens, because none of it is a popup:

- **An app opening.** A pin launches; that is the point of an app folder.
- **An act on the world.** A switch flips its radio, live captions start, a graph opens Task
  Manager, the security widget opens Windows Security, a shortcut opens a page of Settings. An app
  or a window coming up is an act, not a popup — the same line a pin draws.
- **Task view.** The person asked for it in folders too (2026-09-27: "add a shortcut widget to the
  windows windows and desktop overview as well. to the taskbar and to the folder views"). It takes
  the whole screen and is where a window or a desktop is chosen, so its card and its line act: they
  press Win+Tab through the seam the bar's button presses (`Desktops.TaskView`), the widget hands
  the folder nothing to carry out, and the folder may close as Task view takes the screen. On the
  bar it stays a `Panel`; nothing else about the rule changed.
- **The Snipping Tool and Settings** (the backlog, items 10 and 18). Each opens an app of
  Windows' — a snip's overlay, Settings — which is an act, so their cards and lines declare
  `Action` and open what the bar's button opens (`ShortcutTile`). The Snipping Tool missing
  opens its page in the Microsoft Store.
- **A widget's own controls.** A slider dragged, a media button pressed, a device row chosen, a
  countdown's stepper held. These are not clicks on the widget; they never reach the rule.
- **A folder's face on the bar.** It is not in a folder. A click on it opens the folder.
- **A pin to a folder whose navigation shows the contents** (backlog 14 and 28, the person's own
  exception; §32). A pin to a folder has a navigation of its own (`PinOptions.Navigation`,
  `PinFolders`): open the folder in File Explorer, as every pin did; show its contents, one level;
  or all levels deep, each subfolder a list of its own beside its row, as deep as the folders go,
  each opened by a click and never by hovering. It applies to the pinned folder itself where the pin
  shows just the folder, and to each subfolder shown where it shows its contents — the same on the
  taskbar, in a grid folder and in a list folder (the grid's "always File Explorer" is gone). On the
  taskbar the list opens at the button clicked. In a folder of Karpo's, a grid or a list alike, it
  **cascades out of the folder** (`PinFolderBeside`, `FolderFlyoutAction.Beside`): the folder stays
  open, the card, the line or the row clicked stays lit, and the folder's list opens beside the
  panel, level with what was clicked, as a submenu does, so every parent stays in sight (the person:
  "i want it to 'cascade out' so that you can see all the parent folders as well"). One level opens
  that way too now; it used to close a list folder and open where the folder had stood. Each list
  stands beside the row it is the list of, level with it, to the right where there is room and else
  to the left, and once one has gone left the rest go left too (`FlyoutHost.BesideX`), kept on the
  screen. A click on another subfolder of a list closes the lists after it and opens the new one; a
  click on the one already open leaves it; Escape closes the deepest list, the first last; a press
  outside the folder and every list closes them all, and a press on anything else of the folder —
  another line, another row, the space beside the rows — closes the cascade and that press's click
  does what it does. The lists (`PinFolderFlyout`) draw their items as the drive flyout does and
  nothing else — no row of the folder's own, no "Open in File Explorer" at the foot; a folder's row
  has that on its right click — and a file opens with its own program and a folder in File Explorer,
  closing every list (and the folder it came out of), and the row whose list stands open stays lit.
  Which lists stand open is `FolderCascade`, checked without a window (`PinFolderSettingsTests`), and
  `PinFolderFlyoutTests` runs both navigations, four lists deep from every place a folder is clicked,
  and one at the screen's right edge, on a hidden desktop.
  A taskbar button whose click opens such a list has no tooltip, as no entry whose click opens a
  flyout of Karpo's has one (`Dock.OpensFolderFlyout`); one that opens File Explorer keeps its.
- **A right-click.** The rule is about clicks. A right click on a widget opens that widget's own
  menu, which is a menu and not a popup of the widget's, and the folder stays open behind it and
  after it (15.3).

A refused click **does nothing and leaves the folder open.** That is not free: the folder hides
itself before it forwards anything, so a rule asked only where the popup would open would have
shut the folder on the way to nothing.

**What a widget's click does is its own declaration, and the shape it is in decides which answers
there are.** A taskbar entry's (`BarEntry.Click`): `Nothing`, `Action`, `Flyout` (one of Karpo's)
or `Panel` (one of Windows'); the last two are popups. A grid card's and a list line's
