(`GridWidget.Act`, `ListWidget.Act`, a `CellAct`): `Nothing` or `Action`, and no third — a card
and a line have no popup to declare. `Panel` is new with this rule: Start, Search, task view,
second screen and cast had been `Action`, and "Start opens Start" and "show desktop minimises the
windows" were one answer that a rule about popups could not tell apart. The widgets board, the pen
menu, the touch keyboard and the virtual touchpad came later as `Panel`s too. Task view's card and line (2026-09-27) declare `Action`, for the
act above, and so do the Snipping Tool's and Settings', on the bar and in a folder. Second screen
and cast left `Panel` for `Flyout` when they got pages of Karpo's own (§46).

**Where it is enforced: in the types.** Nothing asks a widget where it is.

- The click table (`Dock.Widgets.cs`) is keyed by taskbar entry (`BarKind`), and only the bar's
  path reaches it.
- The folder's path (`FolderFlyout.Activate`) hands the dock one thing, an app opening from a
  widget whose card or line acts (`FolderFlyout.Forwards`), and decides that before it hides, so
  a refused click does not close the folder.
- Second screen and cast open pages of Karpo's own on the bar (§46) and do nothing else, so they are
  taskbar entries only: there is no card and no line of either, and no folder can hold one. The
  mobile hotspot opens its page on the bar too, and in a folder its card and line switch it.

The road that used to take a folder's widget's list of items to the folder — so the folder's own
click would show it — went with the rule rather than being left behind it (`FolderIsland.Forward`).
A road nobody takes is one somebody finds again.

### 15.2 A kind whose face shows nothing cannot be in a folder

Once 15.1 has taken its click, a widget whose face is only a way into something is an inert glyph
in a folder: nothing on it to read, and nothing a click on it will do. So it may not be placed
there at all.

This is a **declared, required fact on every kind** — a face that carries content, or a face
that is only a way into something — so a kind cannot be added without answering it, and one rule
in Core that every path asks: the catalogue's add-into-folder, a drag into a folder, an edit-mode
move and `Repair`. It is not `Surfaces`: a kind on the bar fits a row folder by construction
(`Surfaces.Bar` *is* the row folder), so `Surfaces` cannot take the Wi-Fi button out of a row
folder without breaking the rule that everything on the bar works in a row.

**The classification is with the user before anything is migrated** — the borderline kinds
(the two switchers, the keyboard, Bluetooth, the shell buttons, the tray) are their decision.
Existing configs will have any now-excluded widget moved **out** of its folder onto the bar,
after the folder, with its id and options — never deleted — gated on the file's own version and
idempotent, as every migration here is. That lands once, with the final classification, so the
version gate is set once.

### 15.3 A right click on a widget in a folder is its menu, over the folder

*"implement rightclick context actions for all the grid and list widgets if applicable. (for all
widgets on right click it should not close the folder anymore.)"*

A right click on a card or a line opens that widget's own menu at the pointer, and **the folder
stays open**, in edit mode and out of it: behind the menu while it stands (the folder holds itself
open through the menu taking the focus and through a press elsewhere), and after it, whether it
ended by Escape, by a pick, or by a click elsewhere. A press outside the menu closes the menu alone,
and the next one the folder (§185). A right click between the widgets asks for nothing.

**What the menu holds.** At rest, the widget's icon buttons — Duplicate, Settings (its page in
Karpo's settings, §7b), Remove (§129) — and the kind's own acts; a kind with none has its buttons
alone. While the folder is arranged, the buttons alone, as a widget on the bar has then; "Remove" is
how a widget leaves a folder, at rest as arranged. A pin's menu at rest is the bar's pin menu — its jump list, the app, unpinning, its
"Settings", closing its windows —
with the rows Windows has for a file under the app's own: Run as administrator (for a program),
Open file location, Properties.

**The rule, row by row** (`Dock.WidgetMenus.cs`, one table over every `GridKind` and `ListKind`):
every row acts there and then, or hands Windows something to open. None opens a popup of Karpo's —
the clock's "Notifications" is left off for that — and none does what a click on the widget does
already: the switches' on and off, the graphs' Task Manager, Security's Windows Security, the volume
card's mute, the page nearby sharing and accessibility open on a click. What nothing can do is not
offered: no widget has a forecast's or a quote's page, and mail is read here, not opened. A widget's page in Windows is the one its record names
(`WidgetInfo.Settings`), under the words the settings app shows for it; the sound panel's pieces
take the sound widget's.

Every menu at rest ends with the widget's "Settings" under these rows (§7b), which the table leaves
out; "—" is a menu of "Settings" alone.

| Widget | Its own rows |
| --- | --- |
| Weather, its conditions, a share, mail | Refresh |
| CPU, GPU, memory, disk, network | Resource Monitor |
| Now playing | Play or Pause, Previous track, Next track, Open (the player) |
| Drive | Open, Eject (a stick, a card, a disc), Properties |
| Network drive | Open, Disconnect, Properties |
| Removable devices | Open, Eject, Properties, under each device plugged in |
| Heading | — |
| Calendar | Open Calendar, Refresh |
| Volume (card) | Volume mixer, its page in Windows (Sound) |
| Output devices, the volume row | Mute, Volume mixer, the sound page in Windows |
| Microphones | Mute microphone, the sound page in Windows |
| Mixer | Volume mixer, the sound page in Windows |
| Battery | Energy saver (on or off, through the energy saver widget's own switch), its page in Windows (Power and battery) |
| Airplane mode, mobile hotspot, VPN, energy saver, night light, rotation lock, live captions, do not disturb | Their page in Windows (a click switches them) |
| Nearby sharing, accessibility, Security | — |
| Windows Update | Windows Update settings, Restart options (`ms-settings:windowsupdate-options`) — at the person's word, though a click opens the first: never a restart from Karpo |
| Clock | Adjust date and time |
| Timer, focus time | Start, Pause, Resume or Start again, as the card's button says; Stop; A minute longer, A minute shorter — its steppers, while it is not running |
| Notification list | Clear all, Do not disturb (on or off, through the do not disturb widget's own switch), Notification settings |
| Pin | Run as administrator, Open file location, Properties, in the bar's pin menu |
| Task view | Task view (Win+Tab), New desktop (Win+Ctrl+D) — the one kind whose menu repeats its click: it says what the widget is, over what else Windows does with desktops from there |
| Snipping Tool (on the bar too) | Open Snipping Tool, Snip in 3 seconds, Snip in 10 seconds, Record screen — each greyed where the Snipping Tool installed cannot |
| Settings | — (a click opens Settings) |

A row reads the widget as it is when the menu opens: a toggle is ticked while it is on, a control
is greyed where the widget's own would do nothing, and a row that names a drive or a file acts on
that one. The acts on a widget go through its own controls (the countdown's buttons, the media
buttons, the sound rows' mute), never around them.

**What a pick does to the folder.** One that stays in Karpo — a refresh, a media button, a mute,
energy saver, do not disturb, a countdown's button, clearing the list, an eject, and Duplicate,
Remove, unpinning, closing a pin's windows — leaves it open. One that hands the screen to another program — a Settings page, an app,
File Explorer, Properties, the settings app, Task view, a new desktop, a snip — closes it at rest, as that program taking the focus
would a moment later; while the bar is arranged it stays, as it does through everything then.

## 16. Grid cards at every span

**Removed (2026-10-09, §70).** This section described the grid folder's cards at every span from
one tile to four by four (`GridCard`, `CardFrame`, `CellIsland.CardAtEverySpan`, the per-kind card
layouts and their sheets). The grid folder and every grid widget are gone, and with them all of it.

## 17. The switches do what Windows' own tiles do

*"cant we set airplane mode on system level? or how does the windows taskbar do it?"* A one-button
widget flips the same setting Windows' quick-settings tile flips, through the same road, and follows
it when it is flipped anywhere else — Windows' own panel included. Where Windows' road is not
documented, the one Windows itself takes is preferred to an imitation, and each is written down with
what it was checked against (`QuickSettings\Services`).

- **Airplane mode** is the Radio Management service's system-wide switch, not every radio turned
  off. Windows' Settings and its tile read and set it through `IRadioManager`
  (`GetSystemRadioState`, `SetSystemRadioState`), a COM interface of the service with no public
  documentation, whose shape open tools have used since Windows 8 (`RadioManager.cs` has the slots
  and the GUIDs). The difference is real: the service remembers which radios were on and brings
  those back, and a radio turned on again on the plane stays on, where turning each radio off and
  on could do neither. The state is followed through the value the service writes when it changes
  (`HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\RadioManagement\SystemRadioState`), watched with
  `RegNotifyChangeKeyValue` (`RegistryWatch`), so nothing polls. Every call to the service is on
  the pool: it is a round trip to another process. Where the interface is not there, the radios one
  by one are the fallback (`RadiosAirplane`), and the smoke pass says which road it took.
- **Night light and energy saver** have no API an app may call, and Windows' own tiles do not need
  one: each tile is a handler of the Settings app, a DLL in System32 exporting
  `GetSetting(id)`, whose item's `"Value"` the tile reads and sets (`SettingHandlers.cs`, with the
  ids the tiles are registered under). Karpo goes through the same item. It is undocumented, so
  every call is guarded — the item must say back the id it was asked for, be a switch and hold a
  boolean — and the handlers live on one STA thread of their own with a message loop, because a
  handler finishes starting up on that loop: night light's said it did not apply until its thread
  had pumped messages for half a second. Night light's state is read where the handler writes it
  (the CloudStore value, read as the Bond structure it is, `NightLightBlob`) and watched, so the
  schedule and Windows' own panel redraw it. Energy saver's is its own status, `GUID_ENERGY_SAVER_STATUS`,
  which the dock's window follows (`EnergySaver.cs`): since 24H2 the power status's `SystemStatusFlag`
  says 1 only in high-savings mode, not for energy saver turned on by hand, so it is used only where
  Windows gives no status (before 24H2). The battery's glyph, the status icon, the switch in every view,
  the battery's menu and its flyout all read it, and redraw on the broadcast it comes with. Where the handler
  says night light does not apply — Windows leaves its tile out — the widget is not available.
- **VPN** is the PC's VPN connections as Windows' tile and page list them, through RAS — the
  phonebooks of connections and the service that dials them, which is what Windows' own tile, page
  and list are built on (`Vpn.cs`); `VpnManagementAgent` is not used by Windows and lists nothing to
  an unpackaged app. Every VPN entry of the person's and all users' phonebooks is listed, built-in
  and third-party alike, and followed without polling: `RasConnectionNotification` for a
  connection made or ended anywhere, and a watch on the phonebooks' folders for a profile added or
  removed. On the bar a click opens the list, as the tile's chevron opens its page — each row
  connects or disconnects its connection, and Windows' VPN settings are at the foot — except with one
  connection, where the click switches it, as Windows' split toggle does. A folder opens no list, so
  there a click disconnects what is up, connects the only connection or the one last connected here,
  and otherwise opens Windows' VPN settings rather than guessing which one was meant. A connection
  dials with what Windows saved for it; one that needs the person — a sign-in, a certificate, a
  plug-in's own prompt — is not dialled blind but handed to Windows' settings, whose sign-in asks.
  It is a switch like the others in every other way: its card lights while a connection is up and
  names it, and its line in a list is a switch's line, drawn for the height it is given, naming the
  connection where it says the state (§9, "A line at every height").
- **Rotation lock** is offered only where the PC turns its screen, as Windows leaves its tile out
  elsewhere. What the PC can do is `GetAutoRotationState`, read the way Windows' own handler for the
  tile reads it (`Rotation.cs`): no sensor, or not supported, is no tile at all — the bar's widget
  takes no room and the library greys the row with the reason — and a remote session, several
  screens, docked or folded as a laptop is the tile greyed and locked. The switch is
  `SetAutoRotation`, which user32 exports by ordinal only (2507) and Windows' handler imports that
  way. Windows keeps the state under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\AutoRotation`,
  which is watched, so the lock switched in Windows' own panel redraws the widget.
- **Spatial sound** is the output in use's, as Windows' sound page and its quick settings offer it
  (`Spatial.cs`): off, Windows Sonic for Headphones, and the Dolby Atmos or DTS formats a person has
  installed. What is on is documented (`SpatialAudioDeviceConfiguration`, asked by the output's
  interface path; GUID_NULL is off) and followed, with the default output. What is offered is what
  Windows' page reads, the formats the output's own property store lists, each with whether its app
  is installed; one that is not is left out, as Windows' quick list leaves it out. Switching is
  `SetDefaultSpatialAudioFormatAsync`, which Windows documents for the app that owns a format and
  keeps for Settings otherwise: where it refuses, the widget says so and opens the sound settings,
  where the person chooses. On the bar a click lists the formats, the one in use ticked; in a folder
  a click turns it off, or on again with the format last used.
- **Bluetooth audio devices connect and disconnect** from their card in the Bluetooth page, as
  from Windows' own page (`BluetoothAudio.cs`). There is no Bluetooth API for it; there is a
  documented audio one, and it is what Windows' page, its quick settings and the Sound control panel
  use: a one-shot request (`KSPROPSETID_BtAudio`, `KSPROPERTY_ONESHOT_RECONNECT` and `_DISCONNECT`)
  to the Bluetooth audio driver's filter, reached through Core Audio from each endpoint of the
  device's container, whatever its state. Disconnecting asks every filter the device has, since
  Windows 11 keeps the microphone otherwise; the connection itself is heard from the device watcher,
  and one that does not come within twenty seconds is said on the page. A mouse, a keyboard or a
  phone has no connect in Windows' page, and none here.
- **The Bluetooth page lists paired devices only.** It looks for no new ones (no watcher for
  unpaired devices, so the radio is not kept scanning while the flyout is open); "Add device"
  opens Windows' Bluetooth settings (`ms-settings:bluetooth`, "Add device" heading the page), where
  a new device is found and paired. (Until 2026-10-10 it opened
  `ms-settings-connectabledevices:devicediscovery`, which Windows 11 answers with the Cast panel —
  "when i click add bluetooth device the cast opens".) It stands at the right of the footer band,
  across from "More Bluetooth settings" (`PageLayout.Footer`'s action), so a long list never
  scrolls it away, and it is there whatever the radio says: with the radio off or with none,
  Windows' dialog still says what to do (2026-10-03). A device that reports its battery shows
  Windows' battery glyph filled to the level, in Windows' tenths (`SystemStatus.Describe`), and the
  percentage beside it; the room for both is kept on every row, so the glyphs stand in one column
  and a level arriving late moves no name. That row is the only place Karpo shows a device's
  battery: no card or list line shows one.
- **A Wi-Fi network's Properties** are Windows' own dialog for its saved profile
  (`WlanUIEditProfile`, which `wlanui.dll` exports and `wlanapi.dll` does not: importing it from the
  latter ended the dock on every click). The dialog runs in a Karpo process of its own
  (`Karpo.exe --wifi-properties {adapter} {profile}`, `WifiProperties.cs`), which the dock waits for
  on a thread that lets nothing out; a process that ends any way but well — Windows refused, it
  threw, it crashed — opens Windows' Wi-Fi settings instead. Closing the dialog, with OK, Cancel or
  its close button, is ending well: Windows answers `ERROR_SUCCESS` for all three, and an error
  only where it could not show it (`ERROR_NOT_FOUND`, `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER`). The network
  flyout closes as Properties is clicked, as Windows' list does.
- **The network widget is the cables and Wi-Fi together (2026-10-04).** *"maybe we should then
  rename it to network widget and not just wifi. yes add it [wired connections] so it is comparable
  in features again".* The widget that was "Wi-Fi" is "Network" wherever it is seen: its catalogue
  row, its blurb, its search words ("wifi", "wi-fi", "ethernet", "network", "internet", "lan",
  "cable" among them), its Windows settings link (`ms-settings:network`), the name Narrator gives it
  where it has no connection to say. Its id stays `wifi`, so no saved layout
  changes. The bandwidth graph that was also "Network" is "Network activity" in the catalogue, so
  one list never offers two rows of one name; on its card and its line it still says "Network"
  beside its reading (`PerformanceIsland.Drawn`). The radio's switch in the flyout is still "Wi-Fi".

  The flyout (`WifiPage`, `Wired.cs`) has **one title, Windows' "Wi-Fi"**, with the radio's switch
  and Refresh at its right, as Windows 11's Wi-Fi page has them. The widget's own name is not said
  again over it (2026-10-05: *"the network flyout should not have a separate network title all the
  way on the top. only the wlan one"*): no "Network" title row, and no second "Wi-Fi" heading in
  the list. Each wired adapter whose cable is in has a row first, under the title and above the
  networks, as Windows 10's list of connections had them, one list with the cables at its head: the
  Ethernet glyph (with Windows' warning
  without internet), the network's name in Windows (`INetwork::GetName`, the adapter's own name
  until Windows has one) and "Connected", "No internet" or "Identifying…". Only real hardware
  counts: Ethernet by type, a hardware interface, not a filter's second entry and not a Bluetooth or
  wireless adapter that says it is Ethernet; a VPN or a Hyper-V switch is none of these, and an
  adapter with neither a network nor an address on it (bridged into a virtual switch) has no row.
  Opening a row in place shows its link speed, its IPv4 address and its network profile, each where
  Windows says it, and Properties, which opens Windows' Ethernet settings
  (`ms-settings:network-ethernet`; Windows has no link to one adapter's page) and closes the flyout.
  **There is no Disconnect**: Windows has none for a cable short of turning the adapter off, which
  asks for an administrator. A cable pulled out takes its row with it, as in Windows' list; on a PC
  without Wi-Fi and with no cable in at all, each adapter's row says "Network cable unplugged" so the
  page does not go quiet. A PC without Wi-Fi whose cables are the page has **no title row at all**
  (`WifiPage.Titled`): a "Wi-Fi" title would stand over no Wi-Fi, and "Network" is the one the
  person asked away. Its cables start 8 DIP from the panel's top, as far as the last row stands from
  the footer, and a small line under them says the PC has no Wi-Fi instead of the big notice. A PC
  with neither Wi-Fi nor a wired adapter keeps the "Wi-Fi" title over its "No Wi-Fi adapter"
  notice. The foot is "Network and Internet settings".
  The page hears a cable plugged in or pulled out while it is open (`NotifyIpInterfaceChange`, the
  unicast addresses' notification and Windows' connectivity hint, all on the IP helper's threads and
  only posted on), and reads again every second and a half while a connection is still being
  identified. Everything is read: nothing here changes a connection, and the tests hand the page
  made-up adapters (`SampleWired`).
- **Nothing a test runs switches anything.** Every source is behind a seam the tests hand made-up
  ones to (`AirplaneTests`), and the read-only half is what the published build's smoke pass
  exercises. A live check of a real switch is the person's to allow.

## 18. Do not disturb is Windows' own, and one service

*"Do not disturb (DND) as a service. It is Windows' own DND, the setting Windows 11's notification
center toggles, so Windows stops showing toasts."* Karpo keeps no do not disturb of its own: turning
it on anywhere in Karpo turns it on in Windows, for every toast of every app, and turning it on in
Windows shows everywhere in Karpo.

**How Windows sets it, found by looking.** It is the quiet-hours machinery that Focus assist was,
in the Windows Push Notifications user service. Windows' own notification center
(`Windows.UI.ActionCenter.dll`), its Settings page (`SettingsHandlers_Notifications.dll`) and the
shell in explorer (`twinui.pcshell.dll`) all reference one COM class there, `QuietHoursSettings`,
and its interface `IQuietHoursSettings`; its AppID runs it in `WpnUserService` and its proxy is
registered for other processes. There is no public setter: the documented
`ToastNotificationManagerForUser.NotificationMode` only reads, the focus-session API is a
limited-access feature, and the CloudStore blob behind it only takes effect when the service
restarts. So Karpo calls what Windows' toggle calls, and Windows stays the owner of its setting —
the rule the switches of §17 keep, and for the same reason.
On is the profile in force (`ActiveProfile`) not being the off one; turning it on sets the person's
own choice to `PriorityOnly`, as Windows' toggle does; turning it off sets it back and, where an
automatic rule is what holds it on, turns that rule off until it next comes round. Changes are
heard through the documented `NotificationModeChanged`, and nothing polls. The slots and how they
were measured are at the top of `Karpo.Dock\QuickSettings\Services\DoNotDisturb.cs`.

**One service, read and set by anything** (`DoNotDisturb.Shared`, one per thread like the
notification store): the bell, the list's header, the one-button widget, and whatever comes later —
a focus session that turns it on, an indicator that shows it — so none of them can disagree. Every
call into Windows is on the pool and the news comes back on the dock's thread. A click shows its
answer at once and Windows' answer then stands, a refusal included. Until Windows has answered it
is nothing at all (§11). A run that may not reach the person's world is given a made-up one, and
Windows' own refuses to switch in one as well: no test and no smoke pass can turn it on.

**Edit mode's dim is not the person's do not disturb** (`DoNotDisturb.Dimmed`). The dim is a
window over the whole of every display, and Windows' rule "When using an app in full-screen mode"
takes it for one: do not disturb came on by itself for as long as edit mode lasted, and the status
icons, the bell and the switch showed it (the person, 2026-10-08: "in edit mode the status icons
widget always shows the do not disturb icon even when do not disturb is off"). Edit mode shows the
real states, nothing made up to arrange; so while the dim stands, and until Windows next speaks
after it has gone, a rule's "on" that the dim found off is shown off. The person's own, and one on
before the dim came, show as ever. Windows itself still holds banners back while the dim stands.

**Where it shows.**

- **The bell** is Windows 11's bell with "zZ" while it is on, as the taskbar's is, and keeps its
  count: a notification still arrives in the list while its banner is held back. The count moves to
  the bell's lower corner then, because the upper one is the "zZ", the one thing that says so. The
  cell is the same either way (§12.2).
- **The notification list's header** has the toggle at its end, as Windows 11's does, on the
  accent while it is on; "Clear all" stands before it, and takes a band of its own where the text
  is too large for the three in one. An empty list says Windows' own words while it is on ("Do not
  disturb is on", and what still gets through). A folder's notification list has none of this: it is
  the list alone.
- **The schedule is Windows'.** The list's footer links to it beside "Notification settings", as
  does the widget's own link (`ms-settings:quietmomentsscheduled`, the Notifications page on
  Windows 11); Karpo keeps no second schedule.
- **A widget of its own on all three types**, in night light's family: the one-button widget on
  the bar, a quick-settings tile lit while it is on in a grid, a switch's line in a list, drawn for
  the height it is given (§9, "A line at every height"). Its
  click switches it, which is an act and not a popup, so it is allowed in a folder (§15.1). Its
  tooltip is Windows' own "Do not disturb: on", with what gets through under it.

**Proof.** `DoNotDisturbTests` holds the service on a made-up source: nothing until Windows
answers, a switch at once and Windows' answer standing, a toggle from nothing known, news raised on
the thread that uses it, another thread refused, the widget as the service's switch, and a test
process never given Windows' own. `FlyoutOffscreenTests.Quiet` holds the header's toggle at its end
at 100 to 200 % and up to 225 % text, "Clear all" never over the title or under the toggle, the
footer's two links never overlapping or cut, a click switching it and a refusal opening Windows'
settings, the bell's glyph changing with its cell and its count not; it writes the pictures.

## 19. The notification list is Windows 11's notification center

*"Karpo's notification centre as Windows 11's"*: grouped by app, a toast's buttons and its reply
box, a long one expanded, and clearing that clears Windows' own list. The panel only
(`NotificationsFlyout`); a folder's notification list draws its own lines and cards
(`NotificationPartTile`) and stays newest first, each with its app's icon.

- **Grouped by app.** A heading with the app's icon and name, and on it a × that clears that app's
  notifications; under it the app's notifications, newest first; the apps in the order of their
  newest. A group of more than three shows its newest three and "See more (n)", which opens it
  whole, and "See fewer" folds it again — Windows' own words. A card under a heading has no app
  icon of its own, as Windows' has not: only the toast's own picture, where it has one.
- **Every sender has its name and icon** (`NotificationApps.cs`, 2026-10-11). *"windows defender in
  notifications widget shows up as Windows.xx.Defender ... and also without icon"*: only the Start
  menu was asked, and Windows' own senders (`Windows.Defender.SecurityCenter`,
  `Windows.SystemToast.*`), an app's unlisted entries, toast-only registrations and tray balloons
  are not in it. Now, in order: the Start menu's entry (only where it carries that AUMID);
  `AppUserModelId\<AUMID>` in HKCU then HKLM, DisplayName and IconUri, indirect strings and
  `ms-resource://` resolved with `SHLoadIndirectString`; a package's AppInfo, else its package; a
  balloon's program from `NotifyIconSettings` (by key, or by IconGuid); last a name made from the id
  (`NotificationText.FallbackName`: "Windows" for Windows' own, a dotted id's last real word) and,
  for Windows' own, Windows' default system notification icon. Windows' white glyph icons are drawn
  in the heading's text colour (`Pixels.Mask`), as white would vanish on a light theme. Kept per AUMID.
- **Expanded by Windows' chevron**, beside the time, where there is more to a card than three lines
  show: the rest of its body, or buttons and boxes. Expanded, it shows all of its body, then each
  input — a text box, or a selection a click steps through — under its title, then its buttons, side
  by side where each one's words fit its share of the row and one under another where not, never
  cut. What the panel has opened, expanded and typed is its own (`NotificationView`) and goes when
  it closes.
- **Activation is Windows'** (`ToastActivation.cs`, whose header has the long version). The card
  itself hands its app the toast's launch arguments; a button its own arguments with every input's
  value; Enter in a box sends it with the button it belongs to. A protocol activation launches its
  URI, never a file. Otherwise the app's COM activator is called — found where Windows finds it:
  the Start menu shortcut's `ToastActivatorCLSID`, `AppUserModelId\<AUMID>\CustomActivator`, or
  the package manifest's `ToastNotificationActivation` — with
  `INotificationActivationCallback::Activate(AUMID, arguments, inputs)`; without one, a packaged
  app gets its own activation with the arguments and a desktop app is started from its shortcut
  with the arguments on its command line, as Windows does for a shortcut with a CLSID and no server.
  What brings the app forward closes the list; a background activation leaves it standing. Each
  clears the notification, as Windows' own does. Windows' Dismiss is offered; its snooze is not,
  because only Windows can bring a toast back later. A packaged app's own background task cannot be
  started from outside Windows, so its background button opens the app with its arguments instead.
- **Clearing clears Windows' list.** One, a heading's app, or Clear all go through
  `UserNotificationListener` (`RemoveNotification`, `ClearNotifications`), whose ids are the
  database's. It answers an unpackaged Karpo where Windows' privacy page allows notification access;
  where it does not, Karpo does not ask, and hides the notification in Karpo alone.
- **Nothing a test runs reaches an app or the person's list.** Activation goes through
  `IActivationPlatform` and dismissal through `INotificationRemover`; an isolated run gets an
  activator and a store that reach neither.

**Proof.** `NotificationCentreTests` holds a toast's buttons and inputs read from its XML, the list
grouped by app, every road an activation takes on a made-up platform — the activator with every
input, a packaged app's launch, a desktop app's command line, the app opened, a URI and a refused
file — and dismissals reaching a made-up Windows list. `FlyoutOffscreenTests.Centre` holds the
panel's groups and folds, the chevron at 100 to 200 % and 225 % text with every control inside its
card, and a run: a card expanded, a reply typed and sent with Enter, a heading's × and a card clicked.
It writes `notifications-grouped-*.png` and `notifications-expanded-*.png`.

## 20. What apps say on their buttons

An app button shows more than that its app is open. A window can report the progress of something
long, set an overlay on the button, and a packaged app can set a badge; Windows 11's taskbar draws
all three, and so does Karpo's, on pins and open apps alike, on every bar that shows the app, and on
a window's own button where the bar does not combine them (`AppSignals.cs`, `Scene.Signals.cs`).

### How they arrive

Progress and overlays come through the taskbar list (`ITaskbarList3`), a COM object in the app's
own process. Its `HrInit` looks up the first `Shell_TrayWnd` — Karpo's tray window while it runs —
and that window's `TaskbandHWND` property, and keeps the window it names for the object's life:
every call after that is a message to it. The tray window names Karpo's own band (`Taskband.cs`),
which keeps what the bars draw and passes every call on to Explorer's band, so Explorer's own taskbar
stays right while Karpo runs and after it quits. The tray window is therefore kept whenever a bar
shows app buttons, not only a tray.

What arrives was measured, not guessed: a desktop of its own with a logging stand-in for the band
and a second process calling every method. Progress is posted — the window, and the TBPF flags or
the share done scaled to 0–0xFFFE. The overlay's icon is sent as a copy that is destroyed once the
call returns, so it is drawn at once. Text, the clip and thumbnail buttons are sent in memory from
`SHAllocShared` made for the band's process, which on this Windows is a global atom whose name
("MARC", then the section's handle and the process id, six bits a character) the band decodes
(`DataAtom`); the section is SHAllocShared's header and the data (`BandData`). Passed on as it came,
that memory would name Karpo's process to Explorer — the mistake an appbar message once made
(`AppbarRelay.cs`) — so the band makes it again for Explorer's process and frees it once Explorer has
answered. Everything else goes on as it came: posted, sent, or sent without waiting.

The taskbar list keeps the band it found, so an app that made it before Karpo's band was there
talks to Explorer's, and one that made it while Karpo ran talks to a window gone when Karpo stops.
Explorer's own answer is `TaskbarButtonCreated`, which it sends a window when it makes the window's
button and which makes an app set its progress and overlay again; Karpo sends it to the windows it
lists whenever the band apps should talk to changes — when Karpo's comes, after an Explorer restart,
and when Karpo's goes (`Dock.AskAppsForSignals`).

Badges are rows of Windows' notification store (`NotificationStore.cs`): Type `badge`, a
`<badge value="…"/>` payload, one per app, read with the toasts and matched to a button by its
app's AUMID. "Show badges on taskbar apps" (`TaskbarBadges`) is honoured.

### How they are drawn

As Windows 11's taskbar draws them, which its own resources say (`Taskbar.View`'s `TaskListButton`
in this PC's `resources.pri`): the progress is a WinUI ProgressBar where the running indicator is,
and the indicator gives way to it. It runs in the accent colour (`AccentFillColorDefault`) — not the
green of Windows 7 to 10 —, `SystemFillColorCaution` paused and `SystemFillColorCritical` on an
error, over the ProgressBar's hairline track, along the button's highlight less its corners (a
labelled button's whole length). A run without an end is a piece of it that DWM keeps sliding
along; nothing in Karpo's process runs per frame for it. Up a vertical bar it fills from the
bottom, where text turned down such a bar begins.

A progress with nothing done shows nothing, and the running indicator stays
(`TileSignal.ShowsProgress`, `SignalShape.Shows`): normal, paused or failed at 0 %, or at less than
a pixel of the run. Apps set `TBPF_NORMAL` or a value of 0 long before anything is done, or while
nothing is going on at all (Spotify's window carries one all the time it runs), because an empty
fill is no fill on the taskbar they were written for: Windows 7 to 10 drew nothing of an empty
bar, and Windows 11 shows such a button with its running indicator alone. Drawn as it came, it was
the progress's bare hairline track the width of the button where the indicator should be — the
1-px line under Spotify's pin. A window with nothing done does not hide another window's progress
on the same button, and says nothing to a screen reader. A run without an end always shows.

The overlay is two thirds of the icon (16 DIPs on the taskbar's 24) on its lower right corner,
reaching an eighth of its height past it. A badge is a pill in the accent colour with
`TextOnAccentFillColorPrimary` on it in the same place: a circle for one figure, longer for more,
"99+" past 99, and Windows' status glyphs by name. A badge takes the corner from an overlay; both
are children of the icon's sprite, so they shrink with it when the button is pressed.

A button of several windows shows the overlay set last, and the one it covered when that goes, as
`SetOverlayIcon`'s documentation says; of their progress, the one that needs the person most (an
error, then paused, then running, then busy) and among equals the window used last. A window that
goes takes everything it said with it.

`TileSignal.Spoken` is what a screen reader adds to the button's name: the overlay's description,
the badge ("3 notifications") and the progress ("45 % done", "paused at 70 %").

### Proof

`TaskbandMessagesTests` decodes the atoms and sections the probe logged and holds how each kind of
message is passed on. `TaskbandRoundTripTests` puts Karpo's band between a real app calling
`ITaskbarList3` and a stand-in for Explorer, each a process of its own on a desktop of its own: the
band keeps what the app said, and the stand-in reads every call as Explorer must, from memory made
for its own process, left holding nothing afterwards. `AppSignalsTests` holds the rules per window
and per button, the badges and what is said; `SignalShapeTests` the places and colours;
`SignalSceneTests` the scene's tree against them; `SignalOffscreenTests` draws every state (and
Spotify's, nothing done, with its running indicator), an overlay and badges, dark and light at 100
and 150 % (`app-signals-*.png`). `ThumbBarTests` reads
the toolbars the probe logged, byte for byte, and holds merging, the flags, the places and the
click; `PreviewToolbarTests` clicks the real window list through a fake sender.

### The window list

The list is its cards, and the gap between them and the button it opened from, which is the way up
from the button and keeps it open (`Preview.Bridge`). Only that gap: the popup's window reaches a
few px over the bar, and beside the button that strip is the bar's, so a pointer resting there has
left the list, as one resting in the shadow's room around it has. The gap is as wide as the button,
whether or not the list is above all of it: a list pushed along the bar against the screen's edge is
off its button's middle, and the way up from the part of the button past the list's end runs over
the shadow's room as far as the window reaches (`PreviewLeaveTests`).

**When it opens by pointing** (Settings › General › Window previews › "On hover";
`PreviewHover`, over the bar's timers through `IPreviewTimers`):

- **The wait is a guard, 80 ms**, not Windows' 400 ms hover time. It used to be 420 ms, and that
  wait was nearly all of the delay people saw ("this delay should be made as short as possible"). A
  pointer crossing the bar crosses a 40–48 px button in about 20–50 ms, so 80 ms outlasts a pass on
  the way to the tray or the clock and still reads as instant. Widgets' own hover flyouts
  (`WidgetHover.OpenMs`) keep the 400 ms.
- **With a list up, the next button's comes at once**, as the taskbar's thumbnails move between
  buttons, and across the gap between two buttons as well: the gap is waited out by the grace, not
  by the guard.
- **It closes 380 ms after the pointer left** both the button and the list, which is the time to
  cross from the button up into it; back on the button or in the list within that, it stays.
- **A leave no message told of closes it too.** "sometimes the window preview pops up and does not
  go away again although i am not there with my mouse anymore": the rules above hear the pointer
  through `WM_MOUSEMOVE` and `WM_MOUSELEAVE`, and a leave that never came (tracking lost, capture
  held, a list laid out again under a still pointer, a bar still counting the pointer on its button)
  kept the list up under nothing. While a list is up the bar looks where the cursor really is every
  100 ms (`PreviewHover.Watched`, `DockWindow.PointerHome`): in the list's cards or the way up to
  them, or on the very button it lists, by rectangles alone. Away for the grace, counted from the
  second look so never sooner than 380 ms and at most a look later, the list closes, and a bar that
  still thought the pointer was on it lets it go. A list laid out again keeps its watch as it was,
  so a window renamed every moment can't hold it up. The watch stops with the list.
- **Nothing is made or waited for when it opens.** The popup's window is made, hidden, as soon as
  previews are on (`Dock.WarmPreview`) and kept. The cards and titles are drawn in the same frame the
  window shows; DWM's previews are asked for off the dock's thread afterwards and come in one by one
  as each registers (`ThumbnailBatch`), a frame each where DWM keeps up.
- **Its one animation is an 83 ms fade** on coming up from nothing, and none where Windows'
  animation effects are off (`Look.Animations`) or when it swaps for another button. DWM's own window
  transition is off for it (`DWMWA_TRANSITIONS_FORCEDISABLED`), as it is for the flyouts.

`PreviewHoverTests` holds the guard, the swap, a pointer passing over the buttons, the grace and
the watch (a leave with no message still closes the list) against a clock of its own.

What an app says of its windows' previews shows in Karpo's window list (`Preview.cs`,
`ThumbBar.cs`), arriving through the same band:

- **The thumbnail toolbar** (`ThumbBarAddButtons`, `ThumbBarUpdateButtons`): a count and 540 bytes a
  button — mask, id, image index, a 32-bit icon handle, a 260-character tooltip, flags. An update
  changes only what its mask names, on the buttons with those ids. The buttons stand under the
  preview as 32-DIP squares, centred, closer where seven need it. Hidden ones take no room; a
  disabled one is faint and does nothing; a non-interactive one is a picture; one without a
  background lights up nothing; one that dismisses closes the list. A click goes back as the
  taskbar sends it: `WM_COMMAND` to the window, `THBN_CLICKED` over the id, the window allowed the
  foreground. A button's tooltip shows nowhere (2026-10-09: "the tooltip for the media control
  buttons in the window preview of spotify should be removed", taken for every app's toolbar): it
  is kept as the button's name and its letter tile, never as a pill over the preview.
- **A button's picture** is its icon (`THB_ICON`), or the picture at its index in the image list
  its window set (`ThumbBarSetImageList`, `THB_BITMAP`), which is how Spotify draws previous, play
  and next; with both, the icon, as the taskbar draws it. The icon is the window manager's handle,
  drawn from Karpo's process as it arrives. An image list is memory in the app's process, so what
  reaches the band (`WM_USER+78`, a data atom) is the list written out with `ImageList_Write`, which
  ExplorerFrame imports, for `ImageList_Read`, which Taskbar.dll imports: the band reads it back the
  same way and draws each picture at once. The dock's manifest asks for common controls 6 for that,
  as Explorer has, since version 5 can't read what 6 writes. Only a picture neither gives is a
  letter tile of the tooltip. `ThumbPicturesTests` holds which picture each button ends with, in
  either order of list and toolbar, through a fake of the drawing.
- **Karpo's own media buttons** stay only where the app made no toolbar. The app's buttons are what
  Windows shows; a player that made its own would otherwise show two rows of the same controls, and
  one that made none still gets previous, play and next from its media session.
- **The thumbnail tooltip** (`SetThumbnailTooltip`) is the card's title in place of the window's.
- **The clip** (`SetThumbnailClip`) is all of the window the preview shows: DWM's source rectangle
  over the client area.
- **Tabs** (`RegisterTab`, `UnregisterTab`, `SetTabOrder`): a window that registered tabs is listed
  as its tabs, in their order, each a card with its proxy window's title and DWM's thumbnail of the
  proxy, which is the app's iconic bitmap; choosing one brings the window forward and sends the tab
  `WM_ACTIVATE`, as the taskbar does.

### Not done

`ThumbBarSetImageList` fails inside the app's own process (E_FAIL) before any message leaves it,
with every image list tried, on a desktop without Explorer — so what it sends was not measured, and
the band reads it from what the two DLLs import (above): `WM_USER+78`, and any other sent message
whose data starts with an image list's "IL" header, both passed on as they come. Unproven until
seen with Spotify on the person's PC. `SetThumbnailClip(NULL)` fails the same way (RPC_X_NULL_REF_POINTER) and sends
nothing, so a clip goes only when its window does. `SetTabActive` arrives as the tabs' window and 0,
without the tab, and `SetTabProperties` is passed on unread: the active tab is not marked. An iconic
thumbnail could not be seen on a desktop DWM does not compose, so tabs' pictures are unproven.
Pins inside a folder and the buttons behind "…" show no signals.

## 21. The status icons are what Windows' taskbar shows while something is so

*"add an indicator task bar only widget. (should show all the different indicators that windows
taskbar can show)"*. One taskbar entry, the Status icons (`indicators`), shows the icons Windows 11's
taskbar puts beside its tray while something is so, a cell each, in Windows' order — privacy
(the microphone, the camera, the location and presence sensing in use), then the network (airplane
mode, the mobile hotspot on, a metered connection), then energy saver, do not disturb, and
Windows' update icon: updates waiting, downloading or installing, or a restart waiting to finish
installing them (§21.3). A VPN connected is none of them: Windows shows it
only as a shield on its network icon, and so does Karpo (§21.1). With nothing to say it has no
cells and takes no room, as Windows shows none; like the tray's, its width is what it shows, which
is the one exception §12.2's rule already makes for a widget with nothing to show.

- **What each says and does is Windows'.** A privacy icon's hover names the apps using it
  ("Microphone in use by:" and one app a line), and a click opens the page Windows opens for it —
  the capability's privacy page, Windows Update. Its right click offers that page and, where there
  is one, a way to turn it off (airplane mode, the hotspot, energy saver, do not disturb), above the
  rows every widget has (`IWidgetMenu`). A restart is Windows Update's own to do: "Windows Update
  settings" and "Restart options" (`ms-settings:windowsupdate-options`), never a restart from here.
  Its click opens no flyout of Karpo's, so each icon keeps its hover.
- **Where each is read** is written at the top of `Indicators.cs`. The privacy icons read what the
  capability access manager writes: an app's key under
  `...\CapabilityAccessManager\ConsentStore\<capability>` (the person's and the machine's, a desktop
  app's path written with "#") is using it while its `LastUsedTimeStart` is set and its
  `LastUsedTimeStop` is 0. Windows' own icon asks the same service through a class with no public
  metadata; the keys are watched instead. The rest reuse the switches' sources — the radio service,
  the tethering manager, the power status, do not disturb — the connection's cost, and Windows
  Update's own keys (§21.3). Everything is followed, nothing is polled, and all of it is read off the
  dock's thread.
- **Each icon looks and answers as the network, sound and battery icons do** (*"the status icons
  should be show in the primary color like win11 does it on its taskbar"*). Windows 11 draws every
  one of them in the taskbar's primary text colour, the clock's and its quick-settings icons'
  (`TextFillColorPrimary`; the system's text colour in high contrast): the microphone and the location
  too, not in the accent, and none in a warning colour of its own — energy saver's yellow is the
  battery's. So the status icons, the network, the sound and the battery all take their colour from
  one place (`IslandInk.SystemIcon`, `IndicatorsIsland.InkOf`). Under the pointer each icon lights its
  own square, the size of the network icon's card beside it, not the whole row's card
  (`Scene.LightsItsOwnCell`); a press shrinks that one icon, as it does the network's.
- **Each glyph is Windows' own**, at the tray's size and place (*"the status icons should be show
  in the primary color like win11 does it on its taskbar"*): what read as quieter was the glyphs.
  Each is the Segoe Fluent Icons code point Windows draws for that state, read from its taskbar's
  and Settings' own files (`Indicators.Glyph`; the table of where each came from is at the top of
  `Indicators.cs`). The location is Windows' arrow (E37A), not a pin; the microphone and the
  location in use together are Windows' one icon (F47F) in the microphone's place, its hover naming
  both and its click opening the privacy page, as Windows' does; the camera is the "Camera on"
  flash's camera (E722); energy saver the tray's leaf (F1E8); presence sensing and the hotspot
  Settings' own. Every one is drawn at the size the network, sound and battery icons are
  (`Fit.SystemIcon`: the tray's 16 DIP on the 48-DIP bar) and by its ink in the middle of its square.
  Where Windows has no glyph Karpo keeps its own: Windows shows no sign of a metered connection.
- **A restart waiting wears Windows' red dot** (2026-10-04: *"Restart required: Windows' red dot"*).
  Windows' tray icon for it is an icon file, `WindowsUpdateImportant.ico`: Windows Update's two
  arrows (its glyph in Settings, E895) and a red dot. Read at every size the file carries, the dot is
  half the icon across with its middle three quarters of the way across and down — 8 px at (12, 12)
  in the tray's 16 — and the arrows are cut away about a sixteenth of the icon clear of it. Karpo
  draws it so (`RestartDot`): the glyph in the one colour, cut clear of the dot through a layer's
  mask, and the dot in Windows' critical red, `SystemFillColorCritical` (#C42B1C on light, #FF99A4
  on dark; `IslandInk.Critical`), rather than the file's pure red; in high contrast the system's
  highlight, as every warning of Karpo's (`IndicatorsIsland.DotOf`).
- **The entry wears the card every widget wears** (2026-10-08, §48: *"all the status icons should
  show with primary background"*): in the islands look one card over all its icons, side by side on
  it as any widget's cells are (`Scene.WearsCard`), each still lit on its own square under the
  pointer. It wore a card per icon before, a gap from the next, as the tray's icons did (§51).
- **Its first look is the layout's.** An entry that shows only what is so is never drawn while nothing
  is, so it starts following when the bar first measures it (§11), and what it starts goes to the pool.
- **Not here, because Karpo's bar already has it**: the network, sound and battery icons (widgets of
  their own), and Windows Security and "Safely remove hardware", which are notification icons the
  tray passes on. Windows' own update icon is a notification icon too, but the status icons stand
  for it (§21.3). Windows shows the camera with a flash on the screen rather
  than in its tray; the entry shows it with the others.

`IndicatorsTests` holds the set and its order for a made-up state, each icon shown by its own part of
it alone, each icon's glyph, the microphone and the location together as one icon, what each says,
opens and offers, the apps in use read from usage keys as Windows writes them, the entry taking no
room with nothing to say and a cell per icon otherwise, a click and a menu row acting, the glyph the
network icon's size in the network icon's square, and every icon drawn inside its cell, by its ink
in the middle of it, at 100 and 150 %, dark and light (`KARPO_PNG_DIR\indicators-*.png`).
`StatusIconColourTests` holds each icon's colour to the network, sound and battery icons' in light,
dark and high contrast, as chosen and as the pixels come out, each icon's hover to the network icon's
square, and draws the status icons beside
those three and the tray where the layout puts them, on their cards
(`KARPO_PNG_DIR\status-icons-beside-system-*.png`); the dot's pixels are its own colour there and
everything else the glyph's. `RestartDotTests` holds the dot's place and size to the icon file's,
its colour to Windows' critical red in light, dark and high contrast, the arrows cut clear of it,
and draws it at its size and four times over (`KARPO_PNG_DIR\restart-dot-*.png`).

### 21.1 A VPN is the network icon's shield

*"VPN same like Windows"* (2026-10-04). Windows shows a VPN connected as no icon of its own: its
network icon wears a small shield in its top-left corner. NetworkIcon.dll's own table of glyphs pairs
the shield (`NetworkIconVPNOverlay`, F8C0) with "TopLeftCutout" forms of the network glyphs — Wi-Fi
at two, three and four bars (F8C2, F8C3, F8C4) and the cable (F8CC) — which are the glyph with the
shield's corner and a gap cut away. The shield sits in the em square's top-left corner, so it is
drawn at the network glyph's own size and from its own origin.

- **Karpo's network icon does the same** (`SystemStatus.Compose`, `SystemControlIsland`): while a VPN
  is connected (RAS, as the VPN switch reads it, followed from the dock's start: `SystemStatus`'s VPN
  part) the network glyph and the dimmed arcs under it are their cut forms and the shield is drawn
  over them, in the icon's colour. Wi-Fi at one bar and cellular leave the corner empty and stay as
  they are. Where Windows' table has no form for the shield — no internet, not connected — none is
  drawn, and the glyph stays whole.
- **It is said**: the icon's hover gains "Connected to VPN: Work", and Narrator's name for it
  "…, connected to VPN Work" (`SystemControlIsland.Spoken`, `Dock.Uia`).
- **The status icons have no VPN any more**, and the VPN switch is the widget it was.

`NetworkIconVpnTests` holds the cut forms and the shield for each network with and without a VPN,
none where Windows has none, the hover and Narrator's name, the shield on the network icon alone, and
draws the icon for each network without and with a VPN, the glyph not moving
(`KARPO_PNG_DIR\network-vpn-*.png`). `IndicatorsTests.AVpnIsNoStatusIcon` holds the rest.

### 21.2 Windows Update, a widget of its own: gone (2026-10-08)

The Windows Update widget (`windowsUpdate`: on the taskbar, as a grid card and as a list line) showed
a restart waiting, and when, on its own. The status icons' update icon (§21.3) says all it said and
more, so it is gone at the person's asking, from the registries, the add list, the menus table and
the strings (§48). A file that still holds one loads without it, quietly: a word no registry has is
read past (`TolerantEnumConverter`, `Config.Repair`), and every widget around it stays.

### 21.3 Windows' update icon (2026-10-05)

*"the update available button does not properly show on the bottom right on a default layout. do we
even have a widget for that? if not add that."* Windows 11 shows an icon in the tray, beside the
network, sound and battery icons, while updates are waiting, downloading or installing or a restart
is waiting for them: Windows Update's arrows with a dot, and a click opens Windows Update. Karpo had
it in pieces: the status icons showed a restart, and only where Windows Update's `RebootRequired`
key said so; the Windows Update widget (§21.2, gone since), always shown, read the same.

**What went wrong.** Windows' icon is a notification icon of the update orchestrator's
(`MoNotificationUx.exe` with `MusNotifyIconHandler.dll` in `C:\Windows\UUS\amd64`, one icon at a time),
so it reached Karpo's tray as any app's icon: among the tray's icons or behind the "^", as Windows'
record of it said, drawn from whatever icon handle it gave. And Karpo's own status icon never showed
what it said: on the PC this was built on Windows showed its icon with an orange dot for a driver
installed and waiting for a restart, which sets no `RebootRequired` key, so the status icons said
nothing and the Windows Update widget "No restart needed"; updates waiting, downloading or installing
were never read at all.

**Now** the status icons' update icon is Windows' icon, where Windows puts it:

- **When**: updates waiting (downloaded and not installed, held back on a metered connection, or
  failed and to be tried again), downloading, installing, or a restart waiting — and nothing, taking
  no room, while there is nothing to say (`WindowsUpdate.Shown`).
- **Look**: Windows Update's arrows (E895) with the dot of Windows' own icon file for it, in its place
  and size (`RestartDot`): red for a restart for Windows (`WindowsUpdateImportant.ico`, drawn in
  Windows' critical red as before), orange for a restart for drivers alone (`WindowsUpdateWarning.ico`,
  #FC9A03), blue for updates waiting or under way (`WindowsUpdateSeeker.ico`, #0078D7); the system's
  highlight in high contrast (`WindowsUpdate.Badge`, `RestartDot.Ink(UpdateBadge, …)`).
- **Hover**: short, as the taskbar's: "Updates available", "Downloading updates", "Installing
  updates", "Restart required" (`WindowsUpdate.Status`). A click opens Windows Update
  (`ms-settings:windowsupdate`), which is not a flyout of Karpo's, so the hover stays; the right
  click has "Windows Update settings" and "Restart options". Never a restart from Karpo, nothing
  changed: read only.
- **Where it is read**, all on this PC, watched and never polled, so Karpo's interval for what it
  fetches online has nothing to do with it: the restart keys as before, and the update orchestrator's
  `UpdateStateSnippet` under `...\CurrentVersion\WindowsUpdate\Orchestrator\Diagnostics`, a line of
  JSON it writes each time an action on an update starts or ends — Windows' own update and each
  driver's state (`Downloading`, `Downloaded`, `DownloadBlocked`, `DownloadFailed`, `Installing`,
  `InstallFailed`, `Installed-PendingReboot`, `Installed-Completed`, `PostReboot-Completed`) and when
  (`WindowsUpdateRegistry.OfSnippet`). Work in hand or a restart waiting from before Windows' last
  start is not believed, and updates waiting count for a week from when it last wrote them. The
  Windows Update Agent is not asked: its search goes online.
- **Windows' own icon** is left out of the tray where a bar shows the status icons, which stand for
  it (`WindowsUpdateTray.Held`, `Dock.TrayHeld`), so there is one icon for updates; and where Karpo's
  reading has nothing to say but Windows' icon is there (a check that failed, a version at its end of
  service), the update icon shows Windows' word for it — its hover, and the dot read from its picture
  (`WindowsUpdateTray.BadgeOf`). Where no bar shows the status icons, the tray shows Windows' icon as
  any other, as before; it stays in the settings app's tray page either way.
- **Where**: the status icons are on a new install's bar and a reset's at the right, after the tray
  and the pen and touch keyboard buttons and before the input indicator, network, sound and battery
  (§23.5), and the update icon is the last of them, next to the network icon. A bar somebody already
  has is not changed. Where it lacks them, **Status icons** is in the add list (found by "update" and
  "windows update" too): Edit the taskbar, "+" in the right section, Status icons, and drag it before
  the network icon.

`UpdateIndicatorTests` holds each stage's visibility, glyph, hover and dot, no room with nothing to
say, the click and the menu, Windows' icon as the fallback and left out of the tray, its dot read from
its picture, the snippet read into a stage (the PC's own among them) and old states not believed,
the keys and the snippet as one state, the default bar placing it, and the registries and the add
list; and draws the update icon for each stage (`KARPO_PNG_DIR\update-indicator-{100,150}-{dark,light}.png`).

## 22. A click on nothing in particular ends the editing

*"After clicking into a text field, clicking empty space doesn't take the focus or selection away;
only another text field or navigating does."* Windows 11 takes it away, in its Settings app and in
its flyouts, and so does Karpo now, in both of its surfaces.

- **Karpo's flyouts.** A press on the panel's empty space, or on something that takes no keyboard
  (text, an icon, a row with only a menu), leaves nothing with the keyboard (`QuickPanel`): the
  Wi-Fi key, the search box, a desktop's name show no caret and no selection, and what is typed goes
  nowhere until the box is clicked again. The notification list's reply box already did. A screen
  reader hears it: the focus event is then the panel's own (`Uia.FocusTarget`), where it used to
  hear nothing and go on reading the box.
- **The settings window.** WinUI moves the focus only to what takes it, so the window follows every
  press, handled or not, from where it landed up to the window (`MainWindow`, "Clicking away"). A
  press that meets a control on the way (a box, a button, a switch, a list, a scroll bar, and a
  box made of others, such as a suggestion box with its search button) is that control's; one that
  meets only the page's surface (the page, its scroller, a card that is no button, the side menu)
  takes the focus off whatever had it, to the frame the pages are in, which holds it for that alone:
  nothing is drawn for it, and Tab goes on from there into the page. The rule is
  `Logic\ClickAway.cs`.
- **The title and the bars over the page are surface** (2026-10-03). The breadcrumb's links are
  links, but the rest of it is the page's title: the crumb of the page on show goes nowhere, so the
  button WinUI makes it of counts for nothing (`Pressed.Inert`), and a press on it lets go like a
  press on the page. An InfoBar is surface too; its buttons are controls of their own.
- **Flyouts and dialogs follow their own presses** (2026-10-03). A popup is not under the window's
  root, so a press in the icon picker's flyout (the layouts', a folder's and a pin's) or in a
  dialog never reached the window's handler. Each follows them itself (`MainWindow.FollowPresses`:
  the icon picker's flyout frame, the About and Accounts dialogs), by the same rule up to its own
  surface, and a press on nothing in particular moves the focus to that surface — not out of the
  popup, which would close a flyout. An icon is a button and keeps it.

`ClickAwayTests` holds the rule on the paths a run on a hidden desktop met (a card's empty space,
the side menu, a switch, the suggestion box's search button, the title's crumbs, a bar's words and
its button, the icon picker's frame and an icon), the `--test press-near` hook finds a box in a
popup standing open as well as on the page, and
`QuickFlyoutOffscreenTests.AClickOnEmptySpaceEndsTheEditing` clicks the Wi-Fi key's flyout away and
back at 100 and 150 %, dark and light (`KARPO_PNG_DIR\quick-clickaway-*.png`).

The settings window's suggestion boxes (a weather widget's place, a stock's symbol, a clock's time
zone) put the saved value back only into a box nobody is typing in. An AutoSuggestBox never has
the focus itself, its text box does, so its own `FocusState` says nobody is there while somebody
types; the place and symbol boxes wrote the saved value over every first letter, and the time zone
box selected all again when its list opened, so the next letter replaced the first.
`Logic\SuggestBoxFocus.cs` keeps what the box's bubbled GotFocus and LostFocus say instead
(`SuggestBoxFocusTests`).

## 23. Windows' pins, the defaults and the screens (2026-10-03)

Backlog items 2, 25, 30, 6 and 41.

### 23.1 Pins kept in step with Windows' taskbar (item 2)

- **Where Windows keeps them.** Explorer keeps its pins in
  `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Taskband`, value `Favorites`: one entry
  per pin in the taskbar's order (a byte 0, the length of an item ID list, the list), ended by
  0xFF. A desktop app's entry names its shortcut in
  `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Internet Explorer\Quick Launch\User Pinned\TaskBar`; a packaged app's names
  the app in the Apps folder and has **no shortcut**, which is why reading the folder alone missed
  them. `FavoritesResolve` beside it holds the shortcuts' own link data and is not needed.
  `TaskbandFavorites` reads the value, `WindowsTaskbarPins` turns each entry into the target a Karpo
  pin opens (the shortcut's path, or `shell:AppsFolder\<app id>`) through the shell's own name for
  it. For keeping in step only a **whole** read counts (`WindowsTaskbarPins.Read`,
  `TaskbandFavorites.Targets`): where the value can't be read, or the shell gives no name for one of
  its entries, the read is null and changes nothing, since a short list would forget pins and the
  next whole read would add them again. A new bar's pins come from the same value read as well as
  it can be (`ReadForNewBar`: the entries the shell names, else the folder's shortcuts), so they are
  Windows' own, in its order, packaged apps too.
- **A pin added to Windows** — "Pin to taskbar" in Start, in File Explorer, in an app's jump list,
  or by an installer — goes into every layout a display shows now (`Config.ActiveLayout` of each
  display, each layout once), after the last pin on that layout's **main bar**: the main row, in a
  slot its type shows, in whichever section that pin stands. A pin in the top row of a Top + bottom
  layout, in a slot the type hides (a Dock's main start or end) or in a folder is not where the new
  one goes, since it would not be seen there. Where the main bar has no pin — a layout with no pin
  at all gets one too (2026-10-09: "if someone pins something with windows natively it shows up on
  our bar automatically as well") — it goes into the main row's middle, which every type shows,
  after the open apps standing there, else at the middle's end (the person's rule of 2026-10-05):
  a Taskbar's or Top + bottom's centre, a Dock's one section. Several pins go in Windows' order
  (`WindowsPinSync.Follow`, `Gained`, `AddTo`, `AfterLastPin`). A layout that holds the app
  already, anywhere in it — a hidden slot, the top row, a folder — and by any target, is left alone.
  **Only layouts a display shows now** get it, not every stored layout: a layout put away is the
  person's as they left it, and a pin pinned in Windows while it was away is not added when it
  comes back (it is no longer new by then). The review layout (`widgets-list`,
  `WindowsPinSync.ReviewLayouts`; `widgets-grid` went with the grid, §70) neither get Windows' pins nor count as holding them. A config
  that stands in for the file (`Config.StandsIn`: defaults while it was locked, a recovery) gets
  nothing, and Windows' pins are not even read then: what Windows gained stays gained, and is read
  as soon as the person's own config is in force (`Dock.ReleaseWindowsPins` arms the read), so it
  never goes into defaults a save would merge into their file. All of it is one config: one save and
  one rebuild, however many pins and layouts, and none for a read that gained nothing (a pin
  Windows lost, Karpo's own unpin read back, a change of another value under the key).
- **How fast.** Explorer writes its `Favorites` value (and, for a desktop app, a shortcut in
  `User Pinned\TaskBar`) the moment a pin is made. The dock watches the key
  (`RegNotifyChangeKeyValue`, `RegistryWatch`) and the folder (`FileSystemWatcher`, `*.lnk`) off its
  thread; each change posts `WM_KARPO_PINS`, which arms a timer again (`WINDOWS_PINS_MS`, 600 ms), so
  the pins are read once, 600 ms after the last of a pin's several writes: a pin shows on Karpo's bar
  within about a second. The first look after a start is `WINDOWS_PINS_FIRST_MS` (3 s), for pins
  made while Karpo was not running (`Dock.WindowsPins.cs`). What Windows had is remembered
  across restarts (`windows-pins.txt` in the local folder, `WindowsPinMemory`), so a pin added while
  Karpo was not running is found at the next start. The file is written whole or not at all (a
  temporary file moved over it) between a first and a last line of its own; one left empty or short
  is no memory, and then Windows' pins as they are now are the start, adding nothing. With nothing
  seen yet, the first whole read is the start. And more than `MostGainedAtOnce` (3) pins gained in
  one read is a memory lost or a taskbar put back, not somebody pinning: they are taken as they
  are, none added, and `karpo.log` says so.
- **A pin removed in Karpo** comes off Windows' taskbar once no layout holds it any more
  (`WindowsPinSync.Release`): on the bar, in edit mode, in a folder, in the settings app, or by
  deleting the last layout that held it. **Only an edit made through Karpo** does that:
  - the dock's own edits, unless its config stands in for a file it couldn't read as the person
    left it (`Config.StandsIn`: defaults for a file locked at start, unreadable or deleted while
    running, or anything `Load` had to recover). Comparing such a config with the real file, once it
    reads, is no removal: it would unpin every Windows pin the person's layouts don't hold;
  - the settings app's edits, told from everything else by the log Karpo's own saves keep
    (`config-edits` in the local folder: each save's file before and after, as hashes). A reload is
    `Config.KarposOwnEdit` only when saves of Karpo's alone lead from the file the dock knew to the
    file now, and the file now is what Karpo's last save left; a hand edit, the file deleted or put
    back, a recovery or an import breaks the chain, and so does an older text of Karpo's coming back
    (config.json.bak restored by hand or by a recovery after an undo had led back past it);
  - never a config that replaced the file whole: an import is another PC's pins, not a removal
    (`Config.ReplacedAt`, the mark `ConfigFile.Replace` leaves). The mark is used up only by the
    reload that takes a config (`Config.ReplacedFor`), not by the copy an import keeps beside the
    file first, nor by a reload that met the file Busy or Broken.
- **Taking one off** is Windows' own "Unpin from taskbar" (the verb `taskbarunpin`), asked of the
  item's context menu, on a thread of its own because a context menu loads shell extensions
  (`WindowsPinShell`). Deleting the shortcut does not tell Explorer, and there is no API. Windows
  offers the verb on the app's Apps-folder entry, and for some desktop apps on the shortcut or its
  program instead, so those are asked in turn. The program only where the shortcut is its own app
  (no app id, or the one Windows makes up for it): a web app's shortcut starts its browser, whose
  "Unpin" would take the browser off. Where none of the exact ones offers the verb, nothing is
  unpinned. Explorer's taskbar may be hidden (`Config.HideTaskbar`);
  its pins are still its own and the verb works either way. File Explorer's own pin offers the verb
  on none of them and stays.
- **One app, two targets.** A pin is matched by its target, by a shared app id, or — where one side
  has no app id — by its program, and then only when the other side has no app id either or only
  the one Windows makes up for that program (its path, or its path under a known folder's id,
  `WindowsPinSync.IsDefaultId`). Two app ids are two apps even with one program: a pin of
  `brave.exe` holds neither Brave's web apps nor a Brave shortcut naming an app id of its own.
- **No echo.** Only pins Windows *gained* since it was last read are ever added, and Karpo only ever
  takes pins off. Karpo's own unpin read back is a pin Windows lost, which adds nothing; one Windows
  would not let go of stays in what was seen, so it is not "new" again; and adding Windows' pins to a
  layout releases nothing.
- **Isolated runs never touch them.** The tests and `--smoke` (`Config.IsIsolated`) neither read nor
  change the person's pins; `WindowsPinSyncTests` holds every rule on a made-up store and shell.

### 23.2 Better defaults (item 25)

A new config hides Windows' taskbar (`HideTaskbar`, now on) and never hides Karpo's bar (`Hide`,
now `never`); a word for hiding this build doesn't know reads as `never` too. Every file Karpo
wrote says both values, so no existing config changes: an older default and a choice look the same
in the file, and a choice is never overridden.

**Putting Windows' taskbar back** (2026-10-16: *"the hide the windows taskbar toggle button does not
really work"*). Hiding sets Explorer's taskbar to auto-hide (ABM_SETSTATE) and keeps the person's own
state in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Karpo\taskbar-state`; turning the setting off, quitting, the guard and a crash
set that state again (`Taskbar.TakeOver`, `Taskbar.PutBack`). The record was deleted however the
put-back went, and a takeover with no record kept whatever ABM_GETSTATE said — Karpo's own auto-hide,
wherever an earlier Karpo had left it on — as the person's: from then on, every put-back set auto-hide
again, and with the setting off Explorer's taskbar stayed hidden at the edge (the user's PC: auto-hidden
at every start since 2026-10-14, StuckRects3 saying it was not). Now the record goes only once
Explorer says the state took, and where there is none the person's own is Windows' setting
(StuckRects3, byte 8), which Karpo's ABM_SETSTATE did not change on the user's PC in five hours of
it. Each put-back is a line of the appbar trace (the guard's in karpo.log). `TaskbarStateTests` holds it against a fake Explorer.

### 23.3 The input indicator on a new bar (item 30)

A new bar has the keyboard layout entry where Windows 11 keeps its input indicator: after the tray
(and the pen and touch keyboard buttons, and the status icons), left of the network, sound and battery icons. Placed, it always shows,
with one layout as with several, the layout in use ("ENG CH"): "keyboard layout widget does not
show when i placed it on the taskbar" (2026-10-08). Until 2026-10-10 a new bar got it only where
more than one keyboard layout was installed, as Windows shows its own (`GetKeyboardLayoutList`), so
a PC with one — the person's, Swiss German alone — had a new bar without it; since then every new
bar has it (§23.7).

### 23.4 Same layout on every screen (item 6)

*Gone since §41 (2026-10-07), and not back with the named layouts (2026-10-08): each display shows
the layout chosen for it.*

"Same layout on every display", on the settings app's Displays page (`Config.SameLayoutEverywhere`,
off by default and written only while on). On, a layout chosen on one bar's menu or switcher is
chosen on every display Karpo knows and remembered for the virtual desktop on each; a desktop
brings one layout back everywhere (the first display's that remembered one), and a display seen for
the first time joins the others. Each display keeps its own entry, so turning it off leaves every
display where it is, and turning it on changes nothing until the next choice.

### 23.5 A new install's bar is Windows' taskbar (item 41, 2026-10-05)

*Since §23.7 (2026-10-10) the weather, search (always the box), Task view, the input indicator and
show desktop are on every new bar whatever the switches below say, and a separator stands before
the clock; the alignment, the seconds, the pins and the battery are still followed.*

*"you should make the default layout that shows with new installations as close as possible to how
windows would show it"*. The bar a new config or a reset gets (`Sections.DefaultLayout`) is Windows
11 25H2's taskbar entry by entry, in Windows' order, with what the person changed in Windows'
taskbar settings followed (`WindowsTaskbar`; where each is read is written at the top of
`WindowsTaskbar.cs`):

| Section | Entry | Why |
|---|---|---|
| left | weather | Windows' Widgets button with the weather; off where `TaskbarDa` is 0 |
| middle | Start | always |
| middle | search | `SearchboxTaskbarMode`: the box (§28) at 2 and where it is not set, Windows 11's default; the icon at 1 and 3; none at 0 |
| middle | Task view | `ShowTaskViewButton`, on unless 0 |
| middle | pins | Windows' own taskbar pins, in its order (§23.1); none where it has none; where they can't be read at all, File Explorer, Edge and the Store, the pins Windows gives a new taskbar, those of them this PC has (`WindowsTaskbar.DefaultPins`) |
| middle | open apps | always |
| right | tray | the "^" and the tray's icons |
| right | pen menu, touch keyboard | where Windows would show them (`InputButtons.ForNewBar`) |
| right | status icons | the microphone or location in use, Windows' update icon (§21.3); no room while nothing is (§21) |
| right | input indicator | only with more than one keyboard layout; placed, it always shows (§23.3) |
| right | network, sound, battery | the battery only on a PC with one (`GetSystemPowerStatus`), as Windows shows none without |
| right | date, time | the seconds where `ShowSecondsInSystemClock` is 1 |
| right | notifications | the bell beside the time, as Windows 11 has it |
| right | show desktop | the sliver at the very end; none where `TaskbarSd` is 0 |

- **Left-aligned** (the person's own alignment: `TaskbarAl`, or the value an earlier build kept in
  `taskbar-alignment` before it changed it, until that is put back, §26; centred where neither says), Start, search, Task view, the pins and the apps stand in the left section, the middle is
  empty, and the weather stands before the tray, where Windows moves its Widgets button.
- **Nothing of Karpo's own that Windows has no button for**: the media widget and the disk graph a new
  bar used to get are in the add list. No Copilot button and no Chat: Windows' taskbar has had neither
  since 24H2 (`ShowCopilotButton` and `TaskbarMn` are not read); the Copilot app, where Windows pinned
  it, is one of its pins.
- **Sizes and options** are Windows': the bar 48 DIPs, its icons 24 (`Config.IconDips`), the app
  buttons combined with their labels hidden unless Windows' own `TaskbarGlomLevel` says otherwise
  (`TaskbarApps.FromWindows`), Windows' taskbar hidden and Karpo's never (§23.2). Since §41 it is
  the one layout a new install has, a Taskbar along the bottom holding its strip, in islands.
- **Not done**: network, sound and battery are three entries side by side, each with its own hover
  and flyout, not Windows' one Quick Settings button; the bar has no entry that groups others.
- An isolated config (the tests, `--smoke`) reads none of this and gets Windows' taskbar out of the
  box (`WindowsTaskbar.OutOfTheBox`). `DefaultBarTests`; the pictures
  `default-bar-{windows,left,no-battery}-<look>-<scale>.png`.

### 23.7 Everything of the vanilla taskbar, and separators (2026-10-10)

*"why is there the keyboard selector not in the default layout? i basically want to have everything
of the vanilla taskbar in the default layout. also add separators between the widgets / groups
where it makes sense"*. Why it was missing: §23.5 followed every switch of Windows' own taskbar
settings and §23.3 the keyboard layout count, and on the person's PC Windows has the Widgets button,
Task view and search switched off (`TaskbarDa` 0, `ShowTaskViewButton` 0, `SearchboxTaskbarMode` 0),
one keyboard layout and no battery; their bar, made from that, had none of them.

- **Every button of the vanilla taskbar** (Windows 11 25H2 out of the box), whatever those switches
  say: the weather (the Widgets button), Start, the search box (Windows' default form since 22H2),
  Task view, the pins and the open apps, the tray, the status icons, the input indicator, network,
  sound, battery, the clock and the date presets, the bell and show desktop. `TaskbarDa`,
  `ShowTaskViewButton`, `SearchboxTaskbarMode`, `TaskbarSd` and the layout count are no longer read
